lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P088926, Participatory Irrigation Development Project, loan 7709-PH (IBRD-77090). Loan agreement conformed 7 August 2009. The completion report of 25 April 2019 gives approval on 24 June 2009, effectiveness on 3 November 2009, a mid-term review on 10 May 2013, an original closing date of 31 March 2015 and actual closing on 31 August 2018, after four restructurings (11 February 2015, 24 September 2015, 31 March 2016 and 13 February 2017). The loan was US$70.36 million at approval, revised to US$58,015,957, all of which was disbursed; the borrower put in US$42,844,004, against US$43.23 million planned, and total project cost was US$100,859,961 against US$113.59 million planned. Environmental category: Partial Assessment (B). On safeguards the report says: "Overall, the NIS did not pose large-scale adverse social and environmental impacts, but pertinent safeguards policies were triggered, including Involuntary Resettlement (Operational Policy or OP 4.12), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10), Safety of Dams (OP 4.37), Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), and Pest Management (OP 4.09)." The word "including" is the report's own, so this may not be the full list; the appraisal document's checkbox table does not survive in the Bank's text version of that document. The report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and the quality of monitoring Modest, and rates overall safeguards performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, filed by the Bank under 21 June 2019 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome, Bank performance and monitoring, and rates the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: National Irrigation Administration
companies.role: Implementing agency. A government corporation attached to the Department of Agriculture that builds and runs the Philippines' national irrigation systems and collects irrigation service fees; its Right of Way Management and regional irrigation offices handled the land acquisition, and the project also paid for the staff reduction under its own Rationalization Plan.

cases.community: The project rebuilt 58 national irrigation systems. Land had to be acquired on ten of them. The Bank's completion report counts 960 families: "a total of 960 families, consisting of 401 landowners, 288 informal settlers and 271 owners of crops trees that had encroached into existing canal right of way." Of the informal settlers, "35 families (13 are IPs) have availed of the resettlement sites that NIA and host Local Government Units (LGUs) have provided while the rest opted to relocate on their own or set back their homes from the canal after receiving cash compensation." The borrower’s own annex to the same report describes the same 960 as “960 PAPs whose properties and livelihood opportunities were affected by project construction”, the report’s acronym list defining PAP as project affected person, puts the resettlement sites in Region 5 and Region 11 and says 299 project-affected people handed over 197,767 square metres, about 19.7 hectares, of right of way by deed of donation. Of the 401 landowners, who lost an average of 708 square metres each, 102 took compensation at the prevailing market price and the rest donated their land. The report records "some initial delays in the payment of compensation due to lack of legal supporting documents from claimants and different documentary requirements for the various types of tenurial status", says these "were all settled", and says funds for three absentee claimants were put in a trust account. It says the feedback from landowners who donated was generally positive, and the borrower's annex says living conditions improved, especially for those moved to the resettlement sites. On one system, the Tigman-Hinagyanan-Inarihan River Irrigation System in Camarines Sur, the resettlement action plan of August 2008 counted 204 informal-settler households scattered inside the works area of seven irrigators’ associations on a system that runs through four municipalities of Camarines Sur, of whom 45 said they would vacate and wanted compensation, a project-provided relocation plot and transport help. No document found reports how many of those 204 were moved.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 August 2018. The completion report of April 2019 and the Evaluation Group's review treat the resettlement as finished and rate safeguards performance Satisfactory. Neither document says what the 35 families were paid, where the resettlement sites are, or what became of the 204 households counted on the Camarines Sur system in 2008.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P113844, Metro Manila Wastewater Management Project, loan IBRD 81620-PH of US$275 million to the Land Bank of the Philippines with the guarantee of the Republic of the Philippines, on-lent to the two Metro Manila water concessionaires. The completion report of 23 December 2020 gives approval on 15 May 2012, effectiveness on 19 October 2012, a mid-term review on 30 January 2014, an original closing date of 30 June 2017 and actual closing on 30 June 2020, after closing-date extensions on 14 June 2017 and 27 June 2019. All US$275 million was disbursed; the borrower’s own contribution was US$142,114,000 against US$96.7 million at appraisal and a revised US$228 million, and total project cost was US$417,114,000 against US$371.7 million at appraisal. The project was classified Financial Intermediary Assessment (F) for environmental purposes. The completion report says the project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01) and Natural Habitats (OP 4.04), at paragraph 68, and the involuntary resettlement policy OP 4.12, at paragraph 71, and rates both environmental and social safeguards Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group’s review gives the same three, citing those two paragraphs; the appraisal document’s checkbox table of triggered policies does not survive in the Bank’s text version of that document. The report rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring Substantial; the Evaluation Group's review, filed under 17 November 2021 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome and monitoring but rates Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory, giving as its reason "There were shortcomings in project design." The Muntinlupa subprojects were the Cupang plant (US$27.68 million), the Tunasan plant (US$16.95 million plus US$4.94 million for nutrient removal) and the 4.12 km Muntinlupa conveyance system (US$14.74 million), all three unfinished at loan closing.

companies.name: Dragonhart
companies.role: Contractor for the Muntinlupa sewerage conveyance system, named as such in the land acquisition completion report of May 2018, which records it working with Maynilad and the design consultant on a trenchless pipe-laying option to avoid moving the people living under the Pasong Diablo bridge.

cases.community: Two of the project's sewage plant sites had people living on them. The Bank's completion report says all the land was bought from willing sellers, "including the lot needed for the Tunasan and Cupang STPs, which necessitated the physical displacement of informal settler families", and that the procedures were complied with "including in the relocation of 21 informal settler families in Tunasan STP and in Cupang STP". Its footnote 28 splits that figure: Tunasan 14, Cupang 7. At Tunasan, the resettlement completion report of 8 March 2017 names the 14 households and says their structures were cleared after compensation was agreed and paid. They had no claim on the land: the report quotes the project's own entitlement matrix, "Affected squatters and other informal settlers will not be entitled to compensation for affected land but will be compensated for affected structures and other investments made on the land and relocation assistance." The replacement plots were sold to them, not given: the sellers’ attorney-in-fact parcelled a 2,999.67 square metre lot into 32 square metre plots at 2,000 pesos a square metre, the zonal value, 64,000 pesos a plot, to be paid off over ten years after two rent-free years, at 500 pesos a month for a 32 square metre plot and 1,000 pesos for 64 square metres, with no interest. The report sets out what the landowner gave up and treats it as part of the package: 15,900 pesos a household in transfer and title costs, 16,000 pesos in free use of the land for two years, and 50,614 pesos in forgone interest over the ten years, which it adds to 82,514 pesos a household. The 14 were moved as a group to a site within walking distance of the old one, and the report says the move “would cause no significant socio-economic disruptions or physical adjustments to their usual activities”. Each household also got between 10,000 and 20,000 pesos from the landowner for its house, depending on the structure, 160,000 pesos in all paid on 17 May 2013; physical transfer help worth at least 5,000 pesos in kind rather than cash; and labour to pull their houses down so they could keep the materials. Ten of the 14 were living on the new lot by June 2016; four were not, and the report names them: one family went back to Palawan, one rents near his work in Muntinlupa, one lives with his parents, and one is in Canada and passed his plot to his brother. A Bank due-diligence visit on 20 June 2014 found four things unresolved at the new site: water connections, electricity, safe access in place of a narrow easement, and copies of land titles. An updated plan of 10 November 2014 was published to cover the restoration of those utilities, and the resettlement completion report of 8 March 2017 says it follows the resolution of those measures. It also says that most of the displaced people it interviewed signified contentment with what they received. At Cupang, the resettlement completion report of 28 May 2014 says eight informal-settler households, 44 people, were displaced from the Arevalo-Cruz Estate, which Maynilad bought from seven siblings. Seven of the eight were paid 143,000 pesos between them for the shanties that were removed and signed affidavits of willingness to vacate; the eighth was not moved off the land: Marjorie Solomon’s father, a transient occupant, was sick and could not move, so the landowner paid to rebuild the family’s shanty on the part of the estate that was not sold, less than ten metres from where it stood, and gave 5,000 pesos for the transition. They had been given a notice to vacate by the landowner dated 14 October 2010 and 90 days to take their structures down. On a second parcel bought for the same plant, Elenita Daco’s, a six-door two-storey apartment block and a bungalow were taken down to open access to the plant from Manuel L. Quezon Road, and the families renting them moved out. The report counts them twice and differently: its Table 3 names nine heads of household with 47 household members between them, while its own summary paragraph says “The fifteen (15) households (7 informal settlers and 8 renters) of the properties except for 2 ... left the area after receiving payments from the landowner.” Their rental contracts had expired in 2009 and were never renewed; they were given notice to vacate from September 2012, signed affidavits of willingness to move, and all had gone by January 2013, with more than three months’ notice, a month’s rent each as transition help and the last month’s rent not collected. One of them, Susan Mendones, moved her sari-sari store less than 50 metres. Three years after that, on 25 April 2017, the news site Interaksyon reported that a house in Barangay Cupang collapsed at about three in the morning and two neighbouring houses were damaged, and that “Initial observations pointed to the possibility of ground subsidence as the sewerage project was removing soil nearby”. The same report gives rain as part of the cause: a resident said it had rained through the night, and the report says several days of rain “may have caused softening and mobility of the foundation soil”. It names a contractor of Maynilad, Dragon Health Corporation, as doing the digging, says the contractor assured residents it would shoulder the consequences, and reports that the barangay chairman halted the work for technical assessments. No Bank document mentions that collapse, and no document found says whether the excavation was part of the Bank-financed conveyance system. At loan closing the Bank listed, as social safeguards business still outstanding on that conveyance system, a memorandum of agreement to be concluded "with the owner of the house affected by the Bayanan Pumping Station in Cupang, Muntinlupa"; the same report's appendix describes the same house as one that "will be affected".
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2020 with the Cupang plant 91.99 per cent built, the Tunasan plant 91.57 per cent built and the Muntinlupa conveyance system 90.48 per cent built. The Bank left three social safeguards matters for Maynilad to settle after closing, with six-monthly reports: the construction method at a Valenzuela pumping station, the agreement with the owner of the house at the Bayanan pumping station in Cupang, and negotiations with the landowner on the Tunasan influent line, failing which the line would be re-routed to a steel bridge. The resettlement completion report says the Tunasan households' water and power were restored and titles prepared; no later document was found on the Bayanan house.

cases.community: Eight sites were built on and two of them had people living on them. The Bank's completion report says in its social safeguards annex: "Two of the eight sub-project sites had occupants who were requested to relocate prior to land negotiations and project implementation." At the North Septage Treatment Plant site in Barangay Guitnang Bayan II, San Mateo, Rizal, there were "eleven (11) households (46 persons) ... who were allowed by the former owner to reside in the property"; when he sold it they were asked to go, and the concessionaire "prepared an ARAP and provided relocation assistance to all the displaced households." The plan of 4 March 2005 names them one by one; the heads of the families were former employees of the previous owner and the first on the list, a widow who sold at the public market and kept backyard pigs, had lived there since 1975. They were offered either housing on 24 hectares of the former owner's land in Montalban or a package of 18,000 pesos a family, which the law set at 60 days of the minimum daily wage of 285 pesos, or 17,100 pesos, plus payment for their houses at replacement cost, free transport and the right to take their building materials. The plan says they chose the second option because the money could start a small livelihood, and that some meant to go back to their home provinces in Luzon and the Visayas. It also records that they were consulted before the sale was negotiated in February 2005 and “have agreed that they will vacate the premises once the lot is sold”, puts their average household income at 15,000 pesos a month, and counts four of the eleven households as having arrived in January 2005, a month before its census. It budgeted 198,000 pesos in assistance and 33,000 pesos in transport, and says the families would get at least 60 days' notice before demolition. At the second site, the Road 5 communal septic tank in Barangay Project 6, Quezon City, the completion report says there were 12 households on land owned by the sewerage system, that they "were considered non-poor", and that "they were issued notifications to vacate the property." The relocation was run by the sewerage system with an inter-agency committee that included the Presidential Commission for the Urban Poor and the Commission on Human Rights, and each displaced household was given the standard package of 22,500 pesos, which the report describes as 60 days of the daily minimum wage, plus free hauling of their belongings. The plan written for that site in March 2005 counted three families, not twelve, headed by a former employee of the sewerage system who had been there since 1983, his unemployed cousin there since 1987, and a tricycle driver, unrelated to them, there since 1986; it said their houses sat on top of the septic tanks, that this was a risk to them, that an authority to demolish would be sought from the mayor’s office, and that they had been told in October 2003 of the need to evacuate. The same plan says of those three that they “have expressed their preference for relocation” and that the result of the first dialogues was “positive with the affected families willing to relocate after due assistance”, naming the socialised-housing option rather than the cash package as the one they were willing to take. The completion report also records that all eight sites needed land, that only one private lot was bought outright, and that the rest were handed over by local governments on conditions such as building parks and sports facilities and refurbishing government offices, which the Evaluation Group says may have cost more than buying land.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2012. The completion report rates environmental compliance Satisfactory and says environmental and social policies and procedures were complied with. The Evaluation Group's review of March 2015 rates the project's outcome Unsatisfactory and says the concessionaire "demonstrated lack of realism, during both preparation and implementation, regarding its ability to resolve land acquisition and community resistance issues in a timely manner (or even, in some cases, at all)", that some local governments never delivered land they had promised, and that several planned plants were dropped. Neither document says where the 23 households went or what became of them.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P108768, Mining Sector Institutional Strengthening Technical Assistance Project, credit IDA-44890 (C4489-MN) and grant IDA-H4110 (H411-MN), together SDR 5.72 million, the equivalent of US$9.3 million; the financing agreement was conformed on 7 October 2008. The completion report of 30 March 2017 gives approval on 26 June 2008, effectiveness on 4 May 2009, a mid-term review on 1 November 2011, an original closing date of 31 December 2012 and actual closing on 31 December 2015, with restructurings on 2 July 2012, 10 January 2014 and 30 March 2015; SDR 5.66 million was disbursed. Environmental category B. No safeguard policy was triggered at appraisal. The report says that "following conduct of a safeguards review of the project in 2013, OP/BP 4.12 (Involuntary Resettlement) was triggered retroactively as part of the Restructuring in January 2014. This was in respect of the earlier financing by MSISTAP of the pre-feasibility study for ETT's East Tsankhi coal mine. The relocation of two winter shelters had taken place in 2010 in connection with development of this mine and more resettlements were anticipated to take place as ETT's coal mining operations expanded (albeit notrelated to MSISTAP or the East Tsankhi pre-feasibility study)." The two documents do not say the same thing about cause. The report puts the relocation “in connection with development of this mine”. The Evaluation Group’s review of the report makes the study itself the cause: the policy “was triggered as a result of the relocation of two winter shelters by an activity financed by the project”, and in its supervision section, “Two winter shelters had to be relocated because of a pre-feasibility study financed by the project.” The project then paid for the remedial resettlement action plan and the resettlement policy framework for the mine's operator. The report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, risk to the development outcome Substantial, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review, filed under 22 December 2017 and carrying no date on its own face, agrees on outcome and risk, rates borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and keeps Bank performance at Moderately Satisfactory while saying the report's own rating "should have been Moderately Unsatisfactory" under the harmonised rules.

cases.community: The Bank's technical assistance credit paid for a pre-feasibility study of the East Tsankhi coal mine, and the Bank later decided that this made the resettlement at the mine its business. The remedial resettlement action plan it then financed, drafted in December 2014 by a Mongolian research centre and an Australian consultancy, says the mine area "was the herders' important pasture resource prior to the commencement of East Tsankhi mining operation in 2010." It counts 26 households hit by the mine: "A total of 26 households were impacted by displacement due to ETT company's Eastern Tsankhi mining operation, out of which 2 households received incomplete compensation for physical displacement, however, 17 households impacted by economic displacement have not received any compensation." Two households were moved by the operator and two by a different coal company, and five more were moved by that other company inside a five-kilometre belt; the plan counts nine households physically displaced in all and 17 economically displaced. Of the two the operator moved, both are named. One lost two winter camps, each with its own hand-dug well, and about 1,250 hectares of seasonal pasture; he was given two winter camps by the soum government, 15 million tugrug from the operator and jobs for three of his children, and asked for a well at the new camp; the plan says "The winter camp provided by the company did not have a water well, which makes the winter camp to be impossible to use; thus Erdenebileg's opportunity for herding the livestock for livelihood was limited and he now lives in the soum center." It adds that no inventory of his assets or income was taken at the time, so "whether 15 million tugrugs are adequate to compensate the loss occured has not been properly studied or estimated." The second lost a winter camp, a deep well, about 550 hectares of seasonal pasture, a hot-water facility and a hectare of planted land; he was given 30 million tugrug, a new deep well, a winter camp from the other company and 0.7 hectares from the soum government "after running around for a while". He told the drafters: "The company drilled the deep-water well, but there was no waterbed (old water well provided 5 tons of water per 15 minutes, but new well works for 20 minutes until it dewaters and we need to wait another 3 hours until to regenerate the water). After the displacement, nobody visited us; when we asked about the hot water facility, they responded that the request was submitted to the management, and already 2 years passed." The 17 households who lost summer and autumn grazing were left out of the operator’s resettlement work altogether, and the plan’s table names all 17, two inside the mining licence area and 15 in the five-kilometre zone, with the pasture each lost running from 65 hectares to 2,772 hectares. Against 14 of the names it records “Out-migrated”, against one “Deceased”, and against one that he lost his livestock and settled in a bag centre; the seventeenth name carries no status and her pasture is counted in the same cell as another household’s 2,538 hectares. One of them is quoted: "Before ETT started its mining operation, we used to stay throughout the summer and fall in the southeast of Ulaan Toirom. Since the mining operation started, it became impossible to stay the same area and we moved to Tsagaan Ovoo Bagh." The plan says the exclusion happened because only herders with fixed assets such as winter camps and wells were counted, no cut-off date was ever announced, and the summer and autumn pasture that fattens the animals was treated as nothing. Its evaluation section says: "The company chose one package of compensation and mainly forced the package to the affected persons, therefore affected persons' right to freely choose from various options was limited"; "Committed compensation package was not fully provided, implementation of the compensation was not monitored, and the livelihood support measures were not planned and implemented"; "The post displacement livelihood of the affected persons was not monitored and evaluated. The strategy was to provide the compensation and forget about the affected persons"; and that there is no grievance mechanism. It also notes that the coal haul road to the Chinese border was not considered at all, and that the households of Tsagaan-Ovoo Bagh, a former mine workers’ village, would be affected by dust once the operator piled its tailings nearby from 2015 — a forecast, not a finding, and one the plan sizes twice, at 137 households in its impacts section and “over 100” in its evaluation.
cases.killed_note: The remedial plan lists one of the 17 economically displaced herders, recorded only as Chimid, as deceased. It gives no cause and does not connect the death to the mine.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2015. The remedial resettlement action plan and the resettlement policy framework were prepared and disclosed, both still marked draft, and the Bank treated the amended safeguards covenant as complied with on that basis. No document found says whether the 17 uncompensated households were ever paid, whether the hot-water facility was built, or whether the unusable winter camp was given a well. A cumulative impact assessment for the area, financed by a different Bank credit, was still unfinished when this one closed.

cases.community: In December 2005 traders were moved from the north-eastern side of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road to the western side, to clear space for trucks waiting to be cleared by immigration at the border. The Environmental Management Unit of the Roads Department, which was responsible for applying the lender's resettlement rules, was told only after the move had happened. The abbreviated resettlement plan written afterwards, in May 2006, states that "because of lack of information and sensitization, the provisions outlined in the Resettlement Policy Framework completed during project preparation have not been followed", and that the plan was written to correct that. The plan lists 67 numbered traders by name and national registration number, some names appearing more than once, and puts the number of people at roughly 65: 23 restaurants, 20 grocery stalls, 21 sellers of vegetables, fruit and other goods, one carpentry business and two pay phones. The sums set were 2,590,000 kwacha for each restaurant, 1,390,000 for each grocery, 400,000 for each market seller, 250,000 for the carpentry and 8,000,000 for each pay phone, 113,410,000 kwacha in all. The costs counted were taking down and rebuilding structures, buying materials, business lost during the move, and transport of materials from Chililabombwe 20 km away. The plan says the host community was the same community, because the move was within the same area, and that the facilities used before the move still served the people who were resettled. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says the government's counterpart funding "was not paid on schedule, only six percent of the required commitments per year, causing delays in implementing the Resettlement Action Plan (RAP), and thus negatively impacting the overall project implementation timetable and costs". The same passage adds that the counterpart funding "was fully realized (US$64.3 million) at project closure as per commitment", and the review rates government performance Moderately Satisfactory.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 67 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The abbreviated resettlement plan's compensation table has 67 numbered entries, with three names repeating, and the plan's own text puts "the total number of people involved" at "roughly sixty-five (65)". That figure is approximate and is attached to the people being compensated; the plan's relocation sentence counts nobody, saying only that "some marketeers had been resettled". No figure in any document for this project carries a relocation verb, so none is counted here.
cases.outcome: The plan set out that the contractor would pay each trader in front of a council officer and an officer of the Environmental Management Unit, that each would sign a receipt, and that the signed receipts would go to the Resident Engineer as part of the contractor's monthly claim and on to the Road Development Agency, the National Road Fund Agency and the World Bank. Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it says whether the money was paid. The completion report's table of safeguard documents records the abbreviated plan as disclosed in July 2006. The road was rehabilitated; the Evaluation Group's review says that at closing several sections, among them Chingola-Kasumbalesa, were in poor condition and in further need of repair.

cases.community: The project rebuilt the Kamuzu Barrage on the Shire River at Liwonde. The completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and then records "economic displacement of 22 individual PAPs, 4 institutions (ESCOM, Maritime Police Office, Liwonde Town Council and Liwonde National Park) and 32 Fishermen at both the barrage and SRBA building". The resettlement plan of February 2014 names the people and lists what each stood to lose. One owner faced the complete closure of a camp business on the river, with a boat safari, a bar, restaurants, five guest rooms and twenty campsites. Another faced the replacement of a reception building, a bar, a house, a gate house and an old restaurant, and the loss of business income during construction. A third stood to lose the use of six shops and a dwelling house while the work went on. Eight people are listed, each losing a meat-selling business; the plan lists them as tenants of the town council's shelter and counts them elsewhere as eight households. A bicycle shed, a chip shed and a meat-roasting shed are each listed. Liwonde Town Assembly was to lose the income from six business shelters for three years, and two others the use of bare land, 0.25 and 0.35 hectares, for the three years of construction. The plan records that all of them said they were willing to give up their land provided they were properly compensated, and that they pressed to know when work would start so they could reposition themselves; the valuation team could not tell them. The project's flood-protection structures used voluntary land donation rather than purchase. A grievance system was set up and used, but the completion report says it was "gauged as partially non-inclusive to all PAPs because larger business owners did not use it", and that by project closure one grievance was still unresolved and in the courts. Elsewhere the same report says "all grievances were amicably resolved except one grievance by a lodge owner which is currently in court". The appraisal document also records that the barrage would lower dry-season water levels upstream in Liwonde National Park, reducing sandbars and floodplain grassland, and that the project area included restrictions on access to grazing in protected catchments.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 26 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. The World Bank's completion report says the project's sub-projects did not entail physical relocation, and counts 22 individual people, four institutions and 32 fishermen economically displaced at the barrage and the Shire River Basin Agency building.
cases.killed_note: The completion report's economic annex gives 106 people killed in Malawi's 2015 floods and 60 in the 2019 floods. Those are national flood tolls, used to value the damage the project's flood works were meant to avoid; they are not deaths caused by the works.
cases.outcome: The barrage was finished and the project closed on 31 January 2019 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. One grievance, by a lodge owner, was still in the courts at closing and no document records how it ended. In January 2026 the Malawi Freedom Network reported that lodge owners on the Lake Malawi shore in Mangochi and Salima had sued the National Water Resources Authority and the state generator EGENCO, accusing them of negligence in managing the barrage at Liwonde and saying that this caused flooding along the lake shore. That claim concerns the running of the barrage after the project closed, and it is an allegation in a case that has not been decided.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, first phase (P120370), Credit IDA-52480 of SDR 138.7 million (US$210 million equivalent) to Tanzania and Grant IDA-H8440 of SDR 2.0 million (US$3 million) to the Dar es Salaam Corridor Committee, approved 21 May 2013, effective 26 November 2013, closed 31 December 2020 after two extensions; US$175.4 million disbursed. The rehabilitation of the 137.9 km Mafinga-Igawa section of the Dar es Salaam corridor took 78 per cent of the project's money; for the remaining stretch to the Zambian border at Tunduma the project paid only for feasibility studies, detailed designs and safeguard instruments. The project also financed a one-stop border post at Songwe/Kasumulu on the Malawi border, an inspection station at Vigwaza and works at eight accident black spots. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (28 January 2022); the Evaluation Group rates Bank performance and the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory, records that the project closed with a moderately unsatisfactory rating for safeguards, and says it is not clear how the Bank "addressed the issue of fatalities related to contractors and ensured that such accidents did not repeat".

cases.community: Twenty-four people died along the Mafinga-Igawa road while it was being rehabilitated. The completion report counts 104 accidents on the project road during construction, 13 of them fatal, and says that of the 24 deaths "two were attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment, with the rest due to road crashes". The report puts the rate at 0.06 deaths per kilometre per year, half the Tanzanian average of 0.11 for trunk roads at the time, which it links to the slower speeds through the works, and then calls that rate "undoubtedly shocking". A road safety audit was carried out and its findings went into the road design. The borrower's comments, printed in the same report, dispute the Bank's account: they give the number as 23, say that calling it a large number "is not evidenced", point out that the report itself records the rate as below the national average, and say there is no evidence for the implied conclusion that the contractors' handling of traffic was insufficient for the traffic on the corridor. On land, the report says resettlement plans were prepared and carried out satisfactorily for most of the works, but that problems remained at closing in two places. At the one-stop border post, "compensation and demolition of property required by the implementation occurred prior to clearance of the RAP". At one of the black spot sites, "works began, including displacement without preparation of safeguards instruments by TANROADS and approval by the WB". The Bank says it kept monitoring after the project closed to ensure its resettlement policy was met and the affected people properly compensated, and that it will do so until all the resettlement issues are addressed. Other safeguard failures the report and the review record are a contractor dumping debris in wetlands and blocking water flow, and diversion roads built for the works left unattended, with erosion then affecting more than 20 km along the corridor.
cases.killed_note: The completion report counts 24 deaths along the Mafinga-Igawa road during construction, from 104 accidents of which 13 were fatal. Two are counted here because the report ties them to the contractors: they were "attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment". The other 22 the report puts down to road crashes and they are not counted. The borrower's comments in the same report give the total as 23.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 17 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. No World Bank document for this project counts the people displaced at the border post or at the black spot.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2020 with the border post and the inspection station at Vigwaza still unfinished, to be completed with government money. The time for trucks to cross from Songwe into Malawi rose from 24 hours at appraisal to 72 hours at closing, which the report puts down to the construction still under way and to Covid-19 controls. The resettlement and compensation problems at the border post and at the black spot were unresolved when the project closed, and the project's safeguards rating at closing was Moderately Unsatisfactory.

cases.community: Five people died in three accidents on the drainage works between 2015 and 2020. The completion report says the project "encountered weaknesses on the implementation of health and safety issues which led to three severe accidents and five fatalities". A trespasser who broke into a drainage work site through a gap in the fence fell and drowned on 3 April 2016. Two workers died when the soil collapsed at a deep cut on 8 November 2019. Two passengers on a motorcycle died when it crashed into a dump truck working near the Mwanakwerekwe pond on 22 March 2020. After each accident the project team took statements from contractors, workers, consultants and other witnesses, reported to the lender, and agreed corrective measures; the report says site safety and health management improved after those measures. On land and money, the drainage designs were revised during the project and the number of people affected and the cost came out far above the plan; the government could not pay and no land was available for land-for-land swaps, so the credit paid instead. The report says 605 people were compensated for the drainage and solid waste works, "albeit with some delays". A further 167 people in the buffer zone of the Kibele landfill faced delays and incomplete payment because the government budget ran short; after the lender released another US$550,000, all but three had been paid by 1 April 2021. A footnote records that those three could not be reached through radio, newspapers, village leaders "and so on", and that after the loan account closed at the end of September 2021 the government is obliged to pay them if they come forward to claim. The resettlement plan of December 2018 for drainage system C counted 194 affected households and 162 structures, 30 of them to be taken completely: 141 residential structures, of which 30 would be taken entirely and 111 would lose a wall, a verandah, a foundation, a room, a toilet, an outside kitchen or a septic tank; 12 businesses to be closed and moved, among them six at Sogea and shops at Shaurimoyo, Jitimai and Magogoni; and shelters used by widows, disabled people and people with long illnesses who the plan says would need help to move. The November 2017 plan for the Kibele landfill counted 60 individual landholders, of whom 13 living in occupied dwellings, with 57 household members, were to be moved out of the project area. The municipal council demolished one house, with compensation, to open a route for collection vehicles into a dense settlement where people had been throwing their rubbish into the drain. The Evaluation Group also records that the existing dump site, which the project had assumed would last five years, was closed during the project by community opposition unconnected to the project, after which the council "began open dumping of waste in Ng'ambo settlements causing an environmental and public health crisis".

The report attributes the three accidents to weaknesses in carrying out health and safety measures. The Evaluation Group's review repeats all three accounts.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2021 with an outcome rating of Satisfactory. Three people in the Kibele landfill buffer zone had still not been paid when the loan account closed at the end of September 2021, and the government was notified of its obligation to pay them in future. The completion report says overall safeguards management, occupational health and site safety improved after the accidents.

cases.community: One family lived on the footprint of the power station: a woman of 97, her daughter, the daughter's husband and their granddaughter, with a grandson who lived in Palapye and visited. Their home was two small huts built mainly of scrap and found materials, a store and a fence, on about 2,000 square metres of yard and field. They had three donkeys and a donkey cart, which they used to fetch water from outside, and they lived on firewood, mopane worms and fruit they collected and sold in Palapye and on crops they grew for themselves. The abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009 records that they did not plant their usual food crops that year because they knew they would be moved, and that they were to be compensated for that lost harvest. Two plots were cleared for them about 5 to 6 km from Palapye, each to get a house of 3.4 by 10 metres and a pit latrine; while that was built the family was housed in tents on the plots, and the plan says they were to be moved on 25 May 2009. The family asked to stay about the same distance from Palapye so they could keep travelling there daily and keep their way of living. The plan also records that neither grandchild had ever been to school, and that the husband had no identity card, had tried once to get one and lacked the witnesses he needed. On the transmission line corridors, the completion report records that compensation was paid to informal settlers, that one house had to be demolished with its owner relocated to a nearby town, that those works, including the well fields, had an impact on about 130 households, and that two landowners complained about the compensation terms and about a borehole being moved, both complaints being resolved. The Evaluation Group repeats all of it, and adds that "the project team confirmed a resettlement action plan was prepared and successfully implemented". Five fatal accidents happened at the plant: in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015. All but the December 2013 accident were falls from height; that one the report puts down to poor coordination of repairs, and the March 2015 one was a fall from height during boiler repair work. The completion report says safety remained a serious concern throughout the project, with weaknesses in enforcing safety standards and procedures, a lax safety environment, and weak control of who entered and left the site for much of the construction. An action plan was agreed after the first accident and widened after the second, after which the lender's October 2011 mission "concluded that there was a serious lack of safety observance and enforcement at the site for which the main EPC contractor should take prime responsibility". Only after the third accident did the utility suspend work at height, tighten site security and hire both a safety supervision firm and a separate scaffolding contractor; police officers were deployed to enforce site security. The environment department and the waste management department made frequent site visits and fines were levied on the utility and the contractor for breaches over hygiene, waste disposal, sewage ponds, oil and acid storage and insufficient dust suppression. Noise in parts of the plant exceeded both the contract requirements and industry standards.
cases.displaced_label: people - the family resident on the power station footprint, whose resettlement the completion report records as completed
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 5 for this project. The completion report says "the resettlement of the single family of four began during project preparation and had been completed satisfactorily prior to the start of construction activities", which is where the four is counted from. The abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009 says "one family of four is resident" on the footprint while its census table lists five family members, the fifth living in Palapye with friends and visiting. The plan and the report do not agree on when the move happened: the plan says the family was to be moved on 25 May 2009, and the report says the resettlement was completed before construction started, which the same report dates to 29 April 2009. One further household was moved from a transmission line corridor after its house was demolished.
cases.suppression: Mmegi reported on 8 January 2016 that thirty workers employed by NEPEC 11, a subcontractor at the plant, said they had been retrenched after stopping work in December over safety, pay and their contracts. They said they worked near high-voltage electricity, with dust and chemicals, and at height, without protective equipment, a risk allowance or medical checks, and that they believed they were singled out for raising their rights. The company's translator and secretariat, Jia Zhu, denied the dismissals had anything to do with the stoppage, said most of the work at the plant was finished so fewer workers were needed, and said the company had never given the workers medical examinations, not even when it hired them. The Palapye labour office had not settled the matter and set a hearing for 29 February 2016.
cases.killed_note: The World Bank's completion report records five fatal accidents at the Morupule B construction site, in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015, and gives a cause for each: falls from height in all but the December 2013 accident, which it puts down to poor coordination of repairs. It counts accidents and not people, and gives no number of people killed, so nothing is counted here. Global Energy Monitor's entry on the plant, citing a Mmegi report of 30 July 2015, says at least two Chinese workers died during construction and that some Botswana workers were injured through lax observation of safety principles; that is a floor, reported at second hand, and the Mmegi report itself was not read.
cases.outcome: The plant was built but has run far below what was expected: it was meant to work at an annual capacity factor of about 80 per cent and has not. The completion report rates the project Unsatisfactory on outcome, on Bank performance and on borrower performance, and the risk to the development outcome High, and the Evaluation Group agrees. Emissions from the stacks were not measured reliably because the instruments malfunctioned or were not calibrated, and the report says sulphur oxide emissions were likely to have breached the standards whenever the limestone injection system broke down. Ambient air quality data only became available in August 2015, from a single monitoring station moved over from the older Morupule A plant.

cases.community: The project laid 1,254 km of fibre optic cable across Burundi, reaching 34 communes, and linked 58 government institutions and 14 universities. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says that in Burundi "compensations were paid in full for 8,265 people for a total amount of Burundian Franc (BIF) 105,311,800 (equivalent of approximately US$67,000 in April 2015)", and that "115 people were yet to be paid compensation at project closure". cases.outcome: The network was working when the project closed. cases.community: The landfill at Bajkaj-Palavli needed 3.23 hectares of land. The land acquisition completion report of October 2014 says that covered 21 plots belonging to 20 owners, that the land was used for livestock grazing, and that there were no houses or other structures on it. Its Table 1, headed as per the resettlement plan, names every owner with the size of the plot and the area taken, and a second table repeats the same totals with the number of plots corrected. Four plots were taken in full: Sinan Kuci 892 square metres, Ago Kuci 1,859, Nedin Kuci 2,349 and Shahin Haderi 7,123. In total 32,320 square metres were taken out of 54,235. The report says the land should have been acquired before construction started and was not: "the contractor accessed the land before compensations were paid, which caused tensions, consequently work stoppages at the landfill site from November 2013 to February 2014." It also says the delay came from administrative requirements, including the duty on owners to produce full proof of title, and that the number of plots and the land area first recorded did not match the final figures, so the Council of Ministers had to amend its expropriation decision. Payments were made in early February 2014 after that amendment and the works resumed in mid-February. Total compensation was estimated at 19,547,136 lek, about US$193,920; the report's payment table, dated as of January 2015, lists 15,055,387 lek paid. As of October 2014, 13 of the 20 owners had been paid in full. The report gives two accounts of the remaining seven in the same document: the executive summary says they are "either deceased or living abroad, mostly in Greece", and section 3.2 says seven owners "have not applied for compensation", with migration the reason for three and the death of the proprietor for four. The money for those cases was placed in an escrow account and the report says one family was finalising an inheritance procedure to become eligible. Two further owners were identified as affected by the access road. The report's own monitoring table says the affected people were not dependent on the land, so their incomes were not adversely affected, and that there were no new complaints or community opposition. Three commitments to the villages were recorded as finished in 2014: the road from Bajkaj to Palavli, the two village squares and their entrance roads, and an upgrade of the water supply.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 103 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The landfill documents count 20 land owners and 21 plots and record no houses on the land. The Bank's completion report says the waste transfer station at Himara, the project's other waste site, involved no economic or physical displacement.
cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report or in the land acquisition completion report.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report of 27 April 2016 says that at project closure in March 2015 there were no outstanding social safeguards issues and that the compensation question "was resolved before the project closure date". Its safeguards annex gives different numbers from the borrower's report: it says the acquisition took 3.2 hectares "from 21 project-affected people", that full payments were made in 13 cases, and that in 8 cases the people were deceased or living abroad. The borrower's report of October 2014 gives 20 owners, 13 paid and 7 outstanding. The same annex says a resettlement plan for the landfill construction "was prepared and implemented in compliance with World Bank operational policy (OP 4.12)", and that there had been no new complaints or community opposition to the landfill since April 2014. The landfill was 90 per cent built in October 2014 and the works were completed. The report's payment table lists 13 plots paid and 8 unpaid; two of the unpaid plots carry the same owner's name.

cases.community: The project rebuilt part of the M-03 Kyiv-Kharkiv-Dovzhanskyi road and built three bypasses in Poltava oblast: Pokrovska Bahachka, Krasnohorivka and the first stage of the Poltava bypass. The addendum of 9 December 2017 records a house damaged by the works. It says: "No physical resettlement was induced at any stage of the acquisition. However, one PAP in Krasnogorivka bypass has now approached the local administration for resettlement through replacement of house in the same village (Bilotserkivka) as the walls of the house developed cracks due to ongoing road construction works in the RoW about 10 meters away from the house." The same paragraph says the case "was reviewed, found deserving, and is being considered eligible for relocation and resettlement assistance" under the original plan's entitlement matrix, and that the person was added to the list of affected people because the approved plan had not identified them. Addendum No.2, dated December 2018 on its cover, records an acquisition at the same village for a different reason. It says a design change made after residents and local authorities asked for two cattle passes and local roads so people could move around the village without using the main road "resulted in need for additional acquisition of 3 land plots, 1 house and involuntary resettlement of 1 person in the Bilotserkivka village". It does not mention the cracked walls, and no document says the house acquired is the house that cracked. Its table of the three plots names the owners: two plots registered to Nechay O., one for individual housing, a garage and dacha construction and one for personal farming, and one to the company LLC Lubny ShBU No.9. It then sets out the case in detail. Oleksiy Nechay, born 1940, retired and living on a pension, owns the plot with the house on it; the house is 60 square metres, built in the 1960s, with a summer kitchen beside it. He gave his grandson Sharay Artem power of attorney on 30 August 2018 to negotiate the price and sale, and the grandson was to buy him accommodation in Poltava and move him there himself, so the addendum records that no further relocation help from the road service was needed. The addendum also says that as of 2 October 2018 the contractor had the owners' written consent "to carry out civil works on their land plots before the payment of compensation", and that no works were being done on the plot holding the house. The counts of affected people do not agree between the two addenda. Addendum No.1 gives 106 in the original 2012 plan rising to 124 as of 30 November 2017, covering 113.8947 hectares and an estimated 70,245,919 hryvnia of compensation. Addendum No.2 gives 121 as of the same date, and 122 as of 31 October 2018, reached by adding two affected people on the Bilotserkivka lot and subtracting one on the Poltava bypass, where a plot found to have three heirs was counted as one after they were paid in equal shares. Neither document explains the difference between 124 and 121. The 2017 addendum also records that the grievance system agreed in the loan agreement was not working: "Establishment of GRM procedures for the project as agreed in the Loan agreement and approved RAP was not fully executed due to various constraints including jurisdictional authority to enforce the same." It says awareness of the mechanism among people in the project area "is very low", that dissemination by the local administration "has been very limited", and that this "has led to an increase in the number of grievances submitted when road construction works commenced". Some people went to the administration or the courts instead. The completion report says the resettlement policy was triggered because the works "required land acquisition causing both physical and economic displacement", that the involuntary resettlement rating was downgraded for periods "due to lack of attentiveness and initiatives on the part of the agencies involved in land acquisition to resolve issues", and that it was later upgraded. The same paragraph says social safeguard compliance "was mainly rated as satisfactory and social impact and risk related to land acquisition and resettlement was assessed as moderate".
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 73 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The December 2018 addendum says the design change required one house to be acquired and the involuntary resettlement of one person at Bilotserkivka. No document in the set records that move as having happened: the completion report of 15 February 2022 gives no resettlement count at all.
cases.killed_note: The completion report records deaths at the work sites without counting them: "During project implementation several health and safety related accidents took place in the project construction sites, leading in some of these cases to fatalities." It gives no number, no date and no site, and says reporting of these incidents was inadequate early in the project, so no figure can be entered. The report's only counted death figures are road accident counts: it says fatal accidents on the completed sections fell from 20 a year to a total of 6.
cases.outcome: The road and the bypasses were built and the project closed on 30 June 2021. The completion report says the land acquisition problem that mattered most was the delay in government reimbursement, which was resolved when the Bank agreed to finance the acquisitions from the loan. It records no outcome for the damaged house.

The completion report says the works needed about 749 hectares of land, 382 hectares temporarily and 367 permanently, that 44 per cent of it was public and 56 per cent private, and that it affected 4,061 landowners and 1,036 private plots across 27 settlements, with acquisition starting in October 2007. Compensation to landowners ran from the start of 2012 to 2015 and was finished in March 2015. Four households were left out of that process. The completion report says: "However, in December 2016, four households, consisting of 17 individuals, located on two parcels, were notified about physical displacement due to safety concerns. The World Bank learned of the issue in April 2017, during the social baseline studies for the follow-on GSEP. It turned out that these households were informal (for 20-30 years) residents of pastureland, which were not recognized under the Turkish Expropriation Law and therefore excluded from the LAP." It then says: "Upon intervention by the World Bank, to ensure compliance with OP 4.12, this group was satisfactorily compensated by BOTAS in April 2018 and made eligible for priority hiring during construction and operation periods, before having to vacate the land in December 2018." It says 33 of them "cannot be reached due to living in other cities or residing abroad", so the survey covered the 31 living in the area, that for all 31 the whole parcel was taken because the remainder would not have been usable, and that 18 of them gave farming as their main source of income. Of those surveyed, 19 said the acquisition would affect them positively, 7 said it would have no effect, 2 expected to be affected adversely and 1 was unsure; 16 of those farming the acquired land already had other land. On grievances it says "No specific complaint has been recorded from affected land owners. However, some grievances were received during consultation meetings regarding the remaining part of land after acquisition or damage to lands/crops", which were settled by paying for crop damage. Once the facility was operating the completion report records "a prolonged grievance received from local community members regarding the odor generated from the main facility", for which BOTAS says engineering studies were done and the recommended fix carried out.

Reporting exists on livestock producers at Eskil objecting in 2020 to a brine canal across pasture, but that concerns a later expansion and an objection to a future effect, not this harm. The documents do not say where the four households went or what they were paid.

cases.title: Families moved off the Balakhani landfill and waste pickers who lost it
cases.place: Balakhani, Baku, Azerbaijan
cases.point: The settlement of Balakhani in Baku, as OpenStreetMap records it. The resettlement plan places the landfill next to Boyuk Shor lake and about 3 kilometres from the settlement, and gives no coordinate.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P110679, ARP II Integrated Solid Waste Management Project. Loan 7549-AZ (IBRD-75490, US$29.5 million, agreement conformed 20 May 2009) and additional financing loan 8274-AZ (IBRD-82740, US$47.1 million, agreement 10 January 2014). Approved 17 June 2008, effective 31 July 2009, closed 31 August 2018 against an original closing date of 30 September 2013; US$76.6 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 February 2019 rates the overall outcome Satisfactory and the social safeguards performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's assessment of 13 September 2021 was a field-based Project Performance Assessment Report.

companies.name: Tamiz Shahar JSC
companies.role: The state joint-stock company that took full ownership and management of the Balakhani landfill on 14 October 2009, ran its rehabilitation, and later operated the materials recovery facility and the waste-to-energy plant. The resettlement plan uses that date as the cut-off for establishing who was affected.

cases.community: Six families lived on the Balakhani landfill from 1993 to 2009. The resettlement action plan of May 2011 says they have 14 members in total, that they first lived in tents and picked waste, and that they built housing as they earned. It says they bought a shredder in 2004 and built a workshop, bought a second shredder and a washing line in 2006 and built a second workshop, and kept pigs fed on the waste in sheds made from waste materials. The plan says they had no legal claim to the land, which has been designated for landfilling since 1963 and which it describes as severely polluted by municipal, medical and at times hazardous waste. Before the plan was written the residents wrote complaint letters to senior ministers, to government agencies and to the Bank. The plan says: "The letters resulted in an escalation of grievance between all stakeholders in the project and the eventual awarding of a court order to TS JSC supporting the forcible eviction of the PAP. On the insistence of the World Bank and all Government stakeholders the court order was never enacted." It describes the residents' main grievance as a mistaken belief, "borne from miscommunication and misunderstanding", that they would be moved without compensation, and says the plan process had restored harmonious relations. The project also affected people who did not live on the site but earned a living picking waste there. The completion report of 28 February 2019 counts 144 project-affected people in a 2011 survey, including the six families. It says those living on the site were offered apartments in Baku and those whose livelihoods were affected were offered employment, that "Most continued employment either safely at the landfill, or with Tamiz Shahar in the sorting facility with benefits, including pension", that all employees and registered waste pickers were given helmets, gloves and other clothing, and that Tamiz Shahar held 30 individual meetings with waste pickers between September 2014 and February 2015. It notes the project won the Bank's Europe and Central Asia Vice-Presidential Award in 2014, partly for the way the government engaged with the waste pickers. The Independent Evaluation Group's field assessment of 13 September 2021 gives a different count of what happened to them. It says "Six families living at the landfill site were provided with new housing", and then: "However, only 14 of the 100 to 110 waste pickers accepted Tamiz Shahar JSC's proposal and began to work at the facility. Waste pickers reportedly stated that adhering to the eight-hour workday did not suit their preferences." It continues, in a sentence broken by a page break in the report, that currently, as confirmed by the Independent Evaluation Group mission, "only 11 waste pickers from those who were waste picking before the landfill rehabilitation are working at the Balakhani material recovery facility as employees of Tamiz Shahar JSC". It also says some preferred to keep picking at the landfill, that this is allowed under registration and monitoring with safety equipment in place, and that Tamiz Shahar pays waste pickers for plastic, glass and paper collected at the site.
cases.displaced_label: families who lived on the Balakhani landfill and were provided with new housing, counted by the Independent Evaluation Group's Project Performance Assessment Report of 13 September 2021
cases.displaced_note: The project's resettlement action plan of May 2011 says the six families have 14 members between them, but that figure is in a plan and no outcome document carries it; the outcome documents count families, not people. The completion report of 28 February 2019 says the six families living by the site "were offered apartments in Baku" and that the government compensated "those living on the Balakhani site with improved housing"; the Evaluation Group's assessment of 13 September 2021 says they "were provided with new housing". ICIJ gives 14 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and happens to equal the plan's count of family members; it is not used here. The project's own counts of affected people are larger and do not agree with each other: the completion report gives 144 project-affected people from a 2011 survey, and the Evaluation Group gives 100 to 110 waste pickers.
cases.suppression: A court order granting Tamiz Shahar JSC the forcible eviction of the six resident families was issued after they wrote complaint letters to ministers, government agencies and the World Bank. The resettlement action plan of May 2011 says the order was never carried out, on the insistence of the Bank and all government stakeholders.
cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report, the resettlement action plan or the Independent Evaluation Group's assessment. The resettlement plan discusses health risks from waste picking, including accidental ingestion, without giving any count of harm.
cases.outcome: The landfill was rehabilitated into a sanitary landfill with 20 years of capacity and the project closed in August 2018 having spent US$76.6 million. The six families were given new housing. Of the 100 to 110 waste pickers the Evaluation Group counted, 14 took jobs at the materials recovery facility and 11 were still working there when its mission visited in 2021. Picking at the landfill continues under registration.

cases.title: Orchard cleared and a school built on claimed land, Shkodra and Lezha
cases.place: Mark Lula neighbourhood, Shkodra, Albania, and Lezha
cases.point: The city of Shkodra, as OpenStreetMap records it. The site is in cadastral zone 8594, the Mark Lula neighbourhood; the documents give no coordinate. The second site is at the Beslidhja school in Lezha, about 50 kilometres south.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P078933, Education Excellence and Equity Project. IDA credit 41800, XDR 10.50 million committed and XDR 9.83 million disbursed. Approved 1 June 2006, effective 4 October 2006, closed 30 June 2013 against an original closing date of 31 December 2010; restructured 19 March 2010 and 22 March 2012. The restructuring required the recipient to apply the resettlement policy framework retroactively to expropriation already carried out for school construction at Shkodra and other sites, and the amended financing agreement set 30 April 2010 as the date by which the affected party at Shkodra had to be compensated. The completion report of 28 March 2014 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory. The European Investment Bank and the Council of Europe Development Bank co-financed the wider programme.

companies.name: Ministry of Education and Science
companies.role: The line ministry that ran the project, wrote the resettlement policy framework and the site plans, carried the expropriation files to the Council of Ministers, and was responsible for paying compensation out of the state budget.

companies.name: Municipality of Shkodra
companies.role: The city government that planned the new school on the site and ordered the demolition of what stood on it.

cases.community: The project was not meant to build new schools. The completion report of 28 March 2014 says it became non-compliant with the Bank's resettlement policy in 2008, when it was found that the Bank had approved government investments in new school construction that the financing agreement did not allow. Its safeguards annex says: "Complicating matters, in June 2008, the Municipality of Shkodra ordered demolition of a 5,000 M2 orchard in anticipation of a contract for new school construction. The Municipality alleged that the orchard was public land being used informally by a private individual." The same paragraph says that no new construction had actually begun under the project when the discrepancy was discovered, and the Shkodra site plan says the project did not originally involve the resettlement policy because no new school construction had been contemplated when it was prepared. At the Bank's request the ministry stopped all work on new school construction and agreed to apply the resettlement policy retroactively and take remedial action for the affected party. The site plan of 15 April 2010 gives the detail and a different month. It says that in May 2008 the municipality "demolished the existing improvements on the parcel and removed the agricultural activities being conducted by a local resident". The resident, whose name the plan withholds to protect his privacy, had used the site as a garden for fruit and grapes since the 1990s. The plan says he had built an enclosure of about 4,000 square metres with a concrete-block wall about 2 metres tall and an iron gate, that about 3,600 square metres was planted with grapes and 400 with cherries, that the vines were supported by trellises hung from concrete poles, and that there was a small toolshed on a concrete platform. He used the fruit to make raki and for sale. He went to court in 2008 to establish that the parcel was his; the Shkodra District Court decided in his favour and the Appeals Court overturned that in April 2009, on the ground that his document referred to land in a different neighbourhood. The plan concludes that the state owns the land and he has no legal or legalizable claim, so the policy requires no payment for the land itself, but does require payment for the assets removed, calculated on five years of production and sale of fruit and raki. The amount is withheld from the disclosed version. The plan's own footnotes cut the other way: they estimate he "did not earn more than 5-10% of his annual income from the garden", note that he "still operates a large garden at the site adjacent to his home, a few meters away from the site of the demolished garden", and say the income estimate assumed full retail prices when he consumed or gave away much of the produce. His house was across an alleyway and was not affected, and the plan says he filed no complaint about the amount offered. The completion report says the ministry met the compensation covenant by May 2010. A second site went the same way. The completion report says that in June 2010 the Bank received a complaint that part of the extension of the 9-Year Beslidhja school in Lezha was being built on land restituted to a family, that the Bank asked for all work on that site to stop until the matter was resolved, and that the municipality then decided to expropriate. The ministry's team found that the Hafizi family owned 873 square metres of the land the school stood on. An agreement signed on 1 November 2010 recognised their ownership and allowed the works to resume. The plan of February 2011 values the land at 20,000 lek per square metre, 17,460,000 lek in all, divided between eight named co-owners in shares from one twelfth to one third. The plan says none of the owners lived on the land, had built on it or had cultivated it. The completion report says "ultimately the land owner was fully compensated for the value of the land". A third problem was left unresolved. The completion report says that in 2013 the Bank was told that a small structure next to the Mar Lulaj school in Shkodra, taken to be municipal property due for demolition as part of the school works, was being claimed by a third party. The report says the municipality "closed access to the structure by walling it off to students", that "it was confirmed that the municipality remains in compliance with safeguards policies, although the legal situation of this structure has not yet been clarified", and that if the claim were confirmed the municipality was expected to begin expropriation. It then says: "The contractor, under instructions from the municipality, constructed a wall that prevented access to the structure, and the Bank requested that this be corrected. As of project closing, the current status of this issue was unclear."
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 11 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document in the set counts anyone relocated. The Shkodra plan names one affected person and says his house was not touched; the Lezha plan names eight co-owners and says none of them lived on the land.
cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2013. The Shkodra compensation was paid by May 2010 and the Lezha owners were compensated for the value of their land. The completion report says the closing date was extended in part to make up "the 23-months it took to resolve the safeguards issues", and that two of the schools, Mar Lulaj in Shkodra and Keneta in Durres, were still not finished when the project closed. The claim over the walled-off structure beside the Mar Lulaj school was unresolved at closing.
