cases.title: Pump station built on a Bukhara household's plot before any plan existed
cases.place: Bukhara city, Uzbekistan
cases.point: The city of Bukhara, as OpenStreetMap records it. The plan places the pumping station beside Afrosiyab street, with the gravity and pressure sewer lines running under Afrosiyab and Yangiabad streets, and the household at Sitora street 50. It gives no coordinate.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P112719, Bukhara and Samarkand Sewerage Project. IDA credit 4633-UZ (US$55 million, financing and project agreements conformed 26 November 2009) and additional financing credits 5698-UZ and 5699-UZ (agreements 13 May 2016). Approved 4 August 2009, effective 1 April 2010, closed 30 November 2021 against an original closing date of 31 December 2015; US$132.85 million disbursed of a US$136.82 million project. The completion report of 31 May 2022 rates the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the environmental and social safeguards performance at closing Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Bukhara Regional Production State Enterprise Suvokova
companies.role: The regional state water and sewerage utility for Bukhara, the employer for the Bukhara works and a party to the project agreement with the Bank. The plan calls it the Employer for the contract to rehabilitate the existing sewers in Bukhara city.

cases.community: The resettlement action plan of 18 May 2012, for the contract to rehabilitate existing sewers in Bukhara city, covers a wastewater pumping station of 12 metres by 12 metres, 144 square metres, and the sewer lines running to it. The land it was built on was being used by a householder the plan names as Toychiev Nurjon, of Sitora street number 50, who had no authorised document for it. The plan says the use of the site was granted to the utility by decision number 1067 of 24 August 2010 of the Khokim of Bukhara city, "but unfortunately the nearby householder was informed only verbally about the project". By the time the plan was written the clearing had already happened. It says about 30 metres of the existing fence and the steel entrance gate "have already been dismantled by the contractor with the assistance of the householder worker and stored in the householder stores", and that the brick storage house "was demolished" and its roof, doors and windows and the chicken shelter dismantled and stored the same way. The plot held an old chain-link fence enclosing 1,200 square metres with a steel gate, the fence 88 metres long and 2.5 metres high; a brick store 3.8 by 3.8 by 2.4 metres with a corrugated asbestos roof; a closed steel chicken house; and shrubs, vegetation and trees, for which the plan says there is no accurate count. Because no survey of the planting was done before the works, the compensation was worked backwards from an assumed maximum. The plan says the Bukhara City Beautification Department, as a third party, set the maximum at 21 young plants, and the calculation uses cherry, "the most valuable from the list of fruit trees submitted by the owner": 5 kilograms a year over six years, times 21 trees, times the three years taken for trees to grow back, 1,890 kilograms at 1,200 soums a kilogram, 2,268,000 soums, plus 315,000 soums of labour and gardening costs, 2,583,000 soums for the planting, and a disturbance and inconvenience allowance of 10 per cent on top, 258,300 soums, for a total compensation to the household of 2,841,300 soums. The plan says the store, chicken shelter, fence and gate were to be rebuilt by the utility to a layout agreed with the household, that the contractor was to restore the land, that the household would then be able to cultivate the land around the pumping station, and that the household said no temporary shelter or store was needed while the work went on. An annex to the plan is the household's signed receipt for the cash part of the compensation. The project's resettlement policy framework states that "all compensation and other entitlements will need to be paid prior to proceeding with the civil works", which at this site did not happen. It also says the location of the station was adjusted in consultation with the household to reduce the loss of planting. The completion report of 31 May 2022 says the project had no large-scale resettlement and that most of the works were inside existing facilities or along roads, that four resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out "with adequate compensation paid to project-affected parties by project closing", and then: "However, during implementation, inconsistencies in social safeguard policies were a challenge. For example, there were instances of project-affected persons not being compensated for project impacts on time due to lack of capacity to prepare and implement the Resettlement Action Plans."
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document in the set counts anyone relocated. The household named in the plan lives at a separate address and lost a fence, a store, a chicken shelter and planting, not a dwelling.
cases.killed_note: No death is recorded in the completion report.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 November 2021 after two extensions. The completion report says the four resettlement plans were carried out and compensation paid by closing, with no pending actions, and rates safeguards Moderately Satisfactory. It does not say which affected people were paid late, or how late.

cases.title: Farmland and Cocoa Trees Taken Before Payment on Two Dominican Irrigation Works
cases.place: The Canal Lateral Neyba between the Cuatrifurcación and El Sifón, Neyba and Duvergé, Bahoruco and Independencia provinces; the La Gina irrigation system with the Arroyo Rico and Río Jayán dikes, Miches, El Seibo province; and the Yuna-Cañabón system, Bonao, Monseñor Nouel province, Dominican Republic
cases.point: Neyba, Bahoruco, the town the Canal Lateral Neyba is named after and one of the two municipalities the corrective resettlement plan names for that canal. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The plan for the Yuna-Cañabón works gives grid coordinates for its intake and canal tail, and the La Gina plan gives grid coordinates for the Arroyo Rico and Río Jayán dikes. No document found gives decimal degrees.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Emergency Recovery and Disaster Management Project (P109932), Loan 7546-DO, eighty million dollars, agreement dated 27 May 2008 between the Dominican Republic and the IBRD. The completion report of 22 April 2017 says the project was rated Category B and that "Two policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37)"; it adds that the project did not expect to trigger either social safeguard policy and that only focal points for social safeguards were named in the implementing agencies. The evaluation review of 14 September 2017 gives the final list as Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The Involuntary Resettlement policy was added at a level one restructuring, which the completion report dates to November 2010 and which both the review and the completion report's own restructuring table date to 1 October 2010. That restructuring covered only the activities of CDEEE, the state electricity corporation, which is the project's other implementing agency; it did not create a resettlement instrument for the irrigation works carried out by INDRHI. The evaluation review dates the approval of an additional financing of twenty million dollars, Loan 8098, to 17 November 2011; the completion report says its loan agreement was signed on 18 November 2011, that the loan was terminated when the effectiveness deadline of 17 August 2012 was missed, and that it was reinstated with the deadline extended to 16 November 2012. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, and so does the evaluation review; the review rates efficiency modest and efficacy substantial. The report says that in April 2014 it "appeared that INDRHI, which had limited knowledge of Bank Social Safeguards procedures, had begun expropriating farmers/private land owners in two locations in order to construct new canals/re-route existing canals", that "This situation occurred without the knowledge of the Bank and without the benefit of a project-level Resettlement Policy Framework in place", and that a Bank social specialist later "concluded that all persons who had been expropriated had received proper compensation". It says Resettlement Action Plans and Remedial Action Plans were prepared "although with important delays", were acceptable to the Bank, and that by closing the project was in compliance with OP 4.12. In its section on Bank performance the report says the Bank team "may have anticipated and prevented irregularities that occurred within INDRHI's activities" if the policy had been triggered project-wide in 2010, and that the team "took rapid action when INDRHI was found to be in non-compliance regarding the displacement of people, an element not covered at that time by a Bank pre-approved Resettlement Plan".

companies.name: Instituto Nacional de Recursos Hidráulicos (INDRHI)
companies.role: The Dominican state's water resources institute, which built and rehabilitated the irrigation systems and carried out the expropriations. Its Departamento de Derecho de Vía, the right-of-way department, valued the plots and trees and signed the agreements with owners, working with the project's own execution unit. The corrective plan for the Canal Neyba describes the institute's standing practice: "se procede a las firmas de los permisos y los trabajos se inician sin haber pagado las compensaciones correspondientes" — permits are signed and the works begin without the compensation having been paid. The plan also says the execution unit lacked a thorough knowledge of the Bank's OP 4.12.

companies.name: Hanson – Rodríguez, S.R.L.
companies.role: The firm contracted to supervise the Canal Neyba works. Its survey brigade measured the plots to be expropriated and identified the owners, and passed the figures to the project execution unit (corrective resettlement plans, 11 March 2016).

cases.community:
Four corrective resettlement plans published on 11 March 2016 record what happened to farmers on two irrigation works in the Dominican Republic, and say they were written so that the project would be back in compliance with the World Bank's resettlement policy.

On the Canal Lateral Neyba, between the Cuatrifurcación and El Sifón, a new canal was built alongside the old one and a strip of farmland was taken from private plots. The plan for the next stretch of the canal says the expropriations on this stretch happened before the owners were paid: "Dichas expropiaciones ocurrieron, antes de otorgarles las indemnizaciones correspondientes a todos los propietarios de predios, localizados dentro del tramo del Canal Neyba Km 0.00 hasta Km 5.00." Thirteen plots are listed for the first five kilometres, all held without title. Every one carries 2 February 2014 as the date of expropriation. The first group of seven owners was owed 1,343,870 Dominican pesos; half was paid on 14 May 2014 and the rest on 17 July 2014, the plan saying the institution did not have enough money for a single payment. The second group of six owners was paid on 15 October 2014, eight months after the land was taken. The plots run from 0.15 to 24.31 tareas. The plan says no owner lost a whole plot, that nobody was displaced from the place, that no owner lost their means of support and that each lost only part of their fruit trees. It also says that before the land was taken the amounts had been negotiated and agreements signed with every owner authorising INDRHI to expropriate.

On the next stretch of the same canal, from kilometre 5.00 to kilometre 8.50, the plan says the owners were paid before their plots and crops were occupied, following the recommendations of a World Bank social safeguards mission. Its table lists thirteen cases paid on 9 April 2015 and expropriated on 4 May 2015.

On the La Gina system at Miches, in El Seibo, a strip of land was taken to make an access road for the heavy machinery working on the Arroyo Rico dike, and the crops standing on it were taken permanently. The plan says this happened before the owners were paid, and that the land itself was never paid for: "No se pagaron los Predios ocupados provisionalmente, en razón de que serán devueltos, una vez finalizado el Proyecto" — the plots taken provisionally were not paid for, because they are to be returned when the project ends. Only the fruit trees were compensated. Five cases are listed, all held without title, four expropriated on 10 September 2013 and paid on 28 October 2013, the fifth paid on 10 February 2015.

The same plan records two individual losses. Corrective action was taken for one affected person only, Isidro Peralta Amparo, after 63 cocoa trees were cleared on his land; he could not be reached for months because he lives outside the Dominican Republic, and was consulted and compensated once found. On the Río Jayán front, 63 cocoa trees were cleared to cut a bypass channel and the owner was paid on 16 March 2015. Another owner told the Bank's commission that he and the contractor had counted and agreed 75 cocoa trees, "pero sin embargo al final del proceso se cortaron ciento cincuenta (150) arboles Cacaotales" — in the end 150 cocoa trees were cut. The plan adds that apart from that occasion no further complaints were heard.

On the Yuna-Cañabón system at Bonao, six plots were taken permanently, all held without title, for a new intake and feeder canal. Three were paid on 26 December 2014 and expropriated on 8 January 2015; three were paid on 10 April 2015 and expropriated on 5 May 2015. One plot, held by two brothers, was outstanding and was settled on 28 December 2014.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 128 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found counts people or households relocated. The corrective plans say the opposite: on the Canal Neyba "en ningún caso hubo necesidad de expropiaciones del total de predios, de desplazamiento del lugar" — in no case was a whole plot expropriated or anyone displaced from the place. The completion report puts it the other way in its section on Bank performance, where it says the Bank team took rapid action "when INDRHI was found to be in non-compliance regarding the displacement of people". The report and the plans are not reconciled by any document found. The counts the plans do give are of plots and owners: thirteen plots and thirteen owners on the first five kilometres of the Canal Neyba, thirteen cases on the next three and a half kilometres, five cases at La Gina and six at Bonao.
cases.outcome: The completion report of 22 April 2017 says remedial action plans were prepared for the sites concerned with important delays, that a Bank social specialist concluded everyone expropriated had been properly compensated, and that by closing the project was in compliance with the resettlement policy. The La Gina plan says the land taken provisionally there was not paid for because it is to be returned at the end of the project; no document found records the return. The plan says INDRHI has nothing left to pay on that lot. The project closed on 31 October 2016, having been due to close on 31 December 2012.

The case with people in it is on National Route 34 near the junction with National Route 50, at the access road to Colonia Santa Rosa. The plan names a family that ran a comedor, a canteen, in the line of the road until 2009, and the owner of a depot who occupied the right of way. Its footnote sets out what happened: the canteen operator was served with judicial notice in 2002 that he was in the right of way, a judge ordered his eviction in 2009, and he moved to Saucelito with the support of the municipality. The plan says the works had already been done, and the step still owed to the World Bank was for the roads directorate to send a report from the municipality of Colonia Santa Rosa documenting the relocation of the family that ran the canteen and the measures taken to compensate or support the owner of the depot. A second footnote records that the depot owner is the widow of the man originally sued.

Two further cases on the same route, at the accesses to Embarcación and Aguaray, concern informal occupants of the right of way and a restaurant. The plan marks both for future relocation and requires an abbreviated resettlement plan to be sent to the Bank four months before construction of the access begins.

The other cases are land the works crossed without acquiring it from companies and a municipality: parcels of the oil company YPF at two places in Chubut, where the plan says the works had been done and the roads directorate was to obtain the land by agreement or begin expropriation proceedings, and land of a sugar company near the Calilegua National Park in Jujuy, where a new bridge and an access had been built and the works were still to be declared of public utility. One case in Jujuy was dropped when the works were reformulated.

A separate section covers the Bank's indigenous peoples policy: the rehabilitation and maintenance of a road in Neuquén affects the Namuncurá, Cayulef, Paineo and Cayupan communities, and the plan says those works had not yet been carried out and a plan for indigenous peoples existed in draft, based on a preliminary consultation with the affected communities.

cases.community:
The documents on this loan record two kinds of loss to people in the way of the rural power lines.

Two families were moved. The completion report of 26 December 2013 says that on involuntary resettlement "two cases of families being moved were reported and reviewed" and that the Bank's specialist concluded they had been handled in a satisfactory way. The assessment report of 30 June 2017 repeats it.

More people were owed money for rights of way across their land and had not been paid when the loan closed. The subsidy agreements made the distribution companies responsible for meeting the safeguard requirements. The assessment report says two of the nine companies, Electrocentro and Hidrandina, fell behind. Both the completion report and the assessment report give the position afterwards. The completion report: "DFC-DGER reported that 86 percent of the amount of the right of way payments corresponding to 84 percent of the affected people had been made by July 31, 2013." The assessment report: "By July 31, 2013 (one month after the closing date), DFC-DGER reported that 86 percent of the amount of right-or-way payments, which corresponded to 84 percent of the concerned residents, had been made." So 16 per cent of the residents owed money had not received it a month after the loan closed.

The assessment report sets out why. The contracts with the installation companies did not say clearly who was responsible for the payments or how they were to be arranged. It adds three further obstacles: the absence of land titles, difficulty in locating landowners, and those owners' view that the amount they were owed was not worth the time and expense of cashing it. The completion report attributes the problem in part to the involuntary resettlement framework giving inadequate emphasis to right-of-way payments. It also records the lesson drawn, that right-of-way payments and compensation for the negative impacts of construction should be inside the project cost and written into the contractors' activities.

cases.community:
This loan paid for water and sewerage works in municipalities across Colombia, chosen through an application window that 550 municipalities applied to. Getting the land and the rights of way for the pipes was the problem the project did not plan for. The evaluation review of 18 September 2013 says land acquisition and easement issues "are commonly encountered in water supply and sanitation projects. However, they were not adequately factored into project design."

The mid-term review found what the completion report of 30 March 2012 calls "substantive and procedural issues in the application of involuntary resettlement and indigenous peoples policies". The ministry hired three social specialists to carry out field evaluations and to design a remedial action plan for each sub-project that needed one. An overall social remediation plan was approved on 28 April 2010, five years into a project that closed in March 2011.

The completion report gives the position at closing. A Bank review showed the ministry had completed 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements satisfactorily. The remainder was unfinished: "The SRAP, however, is not complete as the resettlement of two families in the Municipality of Neiva and the legalization of 23 parcels and 84 easements are currently in progress." The report adds that full conformity was not realistic in the short term because most of the parcel and easement cases were caught up in legal and administrative procedures, and that the Bank would keep supervising the borrower's progress. The evaluation review puts the same facts as compensation: "At project closure in March 2011, compensation issues related to the legalization of 23 land parcels and 84 easements were still unresolved."

The ministry's own comments in the completion report say the involuntary resettlement policy framework prepared for the project was unclear, and that although it was committed to completing the requirements in the remaining sub-projects, doing so "had a high cost for the nation".
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives no displacement estimate for this project. No document found counts people or households relocated. The counts are of land: 23 parcels and 84 easements unsettled at closing, out of 103 parcels and 1,177 easements, and two families in the municipality of Neiva whose resettlement the completion report says was in progress rather than done.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2011, having been due to close on 30 April 2009. At closing 23 parcels and 84 easements were unsettled and two families in Neiva were still to be resettled, and the completion report says most of those cases were caught up in legal and administrative procedures. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 December 2016, five years later, repeats the figures of 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements completed satisfactorily and does not say what became of the rest, the two families in Neiva or the unsettled cases. It rates this project's outcome moderately unsatisfactory, against the moderately satisfactory of the completion report and of the evaluation review.

cases.title: A Dennery Family's Land Was Built On Without Consent and Only Their Coconut Trees Were Paid For
cases.place: The north embankment of the Dennery River, Dennery Village, Saint Lucia
cases.point: Dennery, the village on the east coast whose waterfront and river embankment the works protect. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The land acquisition report names the river, the bridge and the families and gives no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD and IDA)
lenders.role: The land acquisition and involuntary resettlement report of 20 February 2007 is headed "LC Disaster Management Project II" and is filed in the World Bank's archive under Additional Financing to the Second St. Lucia Disaster Management Project (P111708), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 15 July 2008. The report says the land acquisition request comes from Component 1 of the project, "Physical Prevention and Mitigation Works", which includes the coastal and flood protection works for Dennery Village, and that the request for additional financing to extend the north embankment "triggers the Bank's Operational Policy 4.12, regarding involuntary resettlement". It says the extension requires 6,039 square metres to be acquired out of total lands of 19,895.77 square metres, that this land is privately owned, and that the government now needs to acquire 30 per cent of the lands so the contractor can proceed. The works that had already been built are the parent project's. A Government of Saint Lucia press release of 7 February 2005 says the government secured 7.5 million dollars from two World Bank agencies for the coastal and flood protection of Dennery Village under the Second St. Lucia Disaster Mitigation Project: an IBRD loan of 3.7 million dollars and an IDA credit of 3.8 million dollars, with bids invited under World Bank guidelines. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under the additional financing number could be reached, and no document found for it states a loan or credit number or an amount.

companies.name: Mirai Construction Company Limited
companies.role: The contractor for the Dennery Coastal Protection Phases 1 and 2, awarded at a contract price of 6,683,042.53 East Caribbean dollars. The report says those works began on 26 July 2005 and were completed in the first week of September 2006, and comprised a 415-metre buried revetment, offshore breakwaters, an armoured berm and landfill. The report also names a second contract, the Dennery River Trou a Leau Ravine Works, awarded to Hippolyte Equipment Services (HES) and completed on 30 July 2007. It does not say which of the two contracts built the length of embankment that crossed the family's land.

companies.name: Smith Warner International
companies.role: The consulting engineers, of Jamaica, who prepared the final design report of October 2003, whose contract was varied in February 2006 so they could carry out a topographical survey of the area, and who supervised the earlier works contract. The report says the portion of the design that needed the family's land was left out of the bill of quantities because of land acquisition issues, and that the ministry considered in hindsight that time would have been saved by better communication at that stage.

cases.community:
On 17 February 2007 a World Bank safeguards specialist met three representatives of the property owners whose land was needed to extend the north embankment of the Dennery River. Seven subdivided plots were represented. The report of that meeting, dated 20 February 2007, records what the owners said about what had already been done to their land.

The owners said their land had been used without their consent or any consultation for transporting, storing and dumping materials, and that their trees had been cut down. One loss is larger than that: "an area belonging to the Biscette - Regis family was used for the construction of the existing embankment without consent or compensation; the only compensation paid was for some coconuts trees that were removed." The family's representative, who speaks for four subdivided plots straddling the land where the embankment already stands and the land still to be acquired, said they were never informed or consulted about the project's designs, and had understood that the embankment would run along the river's edge. The report says the participants also spoke of their sense of helplessness, there being no grievance mechanism and nobody responsible they could take their concerns to. Their first contact with the project's intention to build an embankment, the report says, "was when the trucks and heavy construction equipment passed through or near their property".

The report records a meeting held at the end of January 2007 at which, it says, the contractor explained what his company would do and "stated that the government would expropriate the necessary land with or without their consent".

The same owners are for the works. The report says the participants agreed that the project itself will benefit their properties and the well-being of their town, that they acknowledge the benefits and "are eager to see the works extended and completed as far in advance as possible before this year's June storms", and that they had suggestions drawn from living through Hurricane Debbie and other floods, among them more drains and regular clearing of the existing one, which keeps getting clogged with elephant grass.

The report says the land still to be taken is 6,039 of 19,895.77 square metres for a 180-metre extension, that the original designs of the north embankment were over 90 per cent complete, and that since the designs were drawn in 2002 the owners had put up fences and enclosures on the land to be regraded.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 11 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts people or households moved, and the report describes land taken from plots rather than homes removed. Its counts are of land and plots: three representatives at the meeting, seven subdivided plots represented, four of them the Biscette and Regis branches of one family, and 6,039 square metres of 19,895.77 to be acquired.
cases.outcome: No completion report, evaluation review or later plan filed under the additional financing number could be reached, so no document found says whether the Biscette-Regis family was ever paid for the land the existing embankment stands on, whether the 6,039 square metres were acquired, or whether the 180-metre extension was built. The report of 20 February 2007 says a notice of the land to be affected had been sent for publication and that a valuation of each acquired property would follow a survey, with a tribunal process available for concerns and claims.

sources.title: LC Disaster Management Project II, Land Acquisition and Involuntary Resettlement Report, Saint Lucia, February 15-20, 2007 (RP794)
US $7.5 Million for Dennery Waterfront Protection Project (Government of Saint Lucia press release)

cases.confidence_note: The harm rests on one World Bank document, the land acquisition and involuntary resettlement report of 20 February 2007, and within it on what the owners told the Bank's safeguards specialist at a single meeting. No independent report was found; a search of Saint Lucian news and government sources for the Dennery embankment land returned only material on the project's financing and on later flood works. The Government of Saint Lucia's press release of 7 February 2005 corroborates the financing of the works, not the harm, and comes from the borrower. The embankment that was built across the family's land is the parent project's, the Second St. Lucia Disaster Management Project, not the additional financing under whose number the report is filed; the additional financing was approved in 2008, after the report, and the report was written to support the request for it. The report does not say which of the two works contracts built that length of embankment. No sum is given for what the family lost or for what was paid for the coconut trees.

cases.title: Twenty Dangriga Market Vendors Were Moved Out for Twenty-Six Months and Lost a Quarter of Their Income
cases.place: The Dangriga Municipal Market, Dangriga, Stann Creek District, Belize
cases.point: Dangriga Town, Stann Creek District, the town whose municipal market was rebuilt. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The abbreviated action plan names the market, the slaughterhouse and the Cubanos area and gives no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Belize Municipal Development Project (P111928), Loan 7958-BZ, fifteen million dollars, loan agreement dated 2 December 2010 with Belize. The evaluation review of 5 September 2017 gives the count: "Eight of the Bank's ten safeguard policies were triggered. They were Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04), Forests (OP/BP 4.36), Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11), Indigenous Peoples (OP/BP 4.10), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Projects in Disputed Areas (OP/BP 7.60) and Projects on International Waterways (OP/BP 7.50)." The completion report of 5 June 2017 gives the indigenous peoples policy the number OP/BP 4.11 in its social safeguards paragraph, which is the number of the physical cultural resources policy. Both documents rate the outcome Satisfactory; the report rates the risk to the development outcome Moderate and the review rates it Modest. The report says "Four sites required development of Resettlement Plans. All vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations, or compensated", and rates compliance with the social safeguard policies Satisfactory. The review drops the last three words of that sentence and reports it as "all vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations", and adds that "The Bank project team confirmed to IEG that compliance with all safeguards was achieved for all subprojects by the end of the project", which is a staff statement and not a document. Neither the report nor the review mentions the income loss that the project's own abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 records. The total cost of the market sub-project is given in that plan as 1,519,364.33 Belize dollars, of which 1,475,111.00 from the World Bank loan and 44,253.33, three per cent, from the Dangriga Town Council.

companies.name: Belize Social Investment Fund
companies.role: The statutory fund that ran the project through its Project Implementation Unit, carried out the two evaluations of the vendors' losses and prepared the abbreviated action plan. The plan says the first contractor's works contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013. Channel 5 Belize reported on 30 January 2014 that work stopped amid allegations of an incompetent contractor and corruption at the fund, and Amandala reported on 4 April 2014 that four fund employees were dismissed after the first contractor alleged extortion in September 2013, and that the employees denied the claims.

companies.name: Dangriga Town Council
companies.role: The town council, which sought the funding to expand the market, put up three per cent of the sub-project cost, housed the displaced cooked-food and meat vendors in the renovated slaughterhouse and paid their utilities there, and operates the one-stall-per-family policy that the plan says affects five families, who are to be compensated with temporary stalls beside the Cubanos area. The plan says the council agreed to meet 14,990.68 Belize dollars of utility costs and 24,530.00 in stall-fee arrears for all the temporarily relocated vendors.

companies.name: K & G Construction
companies.role: The first contractor on the market works, whose principal the plan names as Mr Smart and whom Amandala names as Kenard Smart. The plan says his contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013 after works that had run from June 2012, and that during his tenure job openings for Dangriga residents were very limited, with more than 75 per cent of workers coming from outside the Stann Creek District. Channel 5 Belize reported on 23 October 2014 that he had been paid about 800,000 Belize dollars before work stopped.

companies.name: CB Construction
companies.role: The second contractor, of San Ignacio in the Cayo District, which took over the works. Amandala reported on 4 April 2014 that the contract was signed on 24 March 2014 for 1,228,310.95 Belize dollars with a pledge to finish in six months. The plan says civil works resumed in April 2014, and that in July 2014 about 12 of a workforce of 17 were Dangriga residents.

companies.name: Anthony Thurton & Associates
companies.role: The engineering consultancy that completed the final drawings and designs for the new market extension, which was to hold 22 new stalls with metal shutters (abbreviated action plan, 20 August 2014).

cases.community:
To rebuild and extend the Dangriga municipal market, the main market building was emptied. The abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 says a joint decision was taken to vacate it during the works because heavy equipment was operating next to vendors and the buying public. Those moved out were the stall owners inside the market, those under the market awnings, those in the fish section and those between the market and the Cubanos area.

Then the works stopped. The plan says the first contractor's contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013 and the civil works did not resume until April 2014, a seven-month gap. A second evaluation was carried out with the vendors who had been moved, to see whether they were losing income because of the delay. Its result: "Initially, a total of twenty (20) vendors were temporarily relocated but this number was reduced to twelve (12) by July 2014 with the majority of them relocating to other locations of the municipality where they are more visible to the buying public. The results of the second evaluation are that on an average, the vendors were experiencing income losses of 25%." The plan's own table gives the length of relocation for those 20 as 26 months, and marks each of their losses moderate.

The first evaluation, reported in April 2011, had concluded that most of the stall owners who would be moved "would not be experiencing any major loss of income sources or means of livelihood".

On 30 January 2014, while the works were still stopped, Channel 5 Belize reported Mayor Gilbert Swaso saying that vendors had lost about 25 per cent of their income while the market was closed, and that the community had lost its market. The same report said the shortfall of about 450,000 Belize dollars needed to finish the market would be taken from a 1.5 million dollar allocation for road works in Dangriga's phase two, money the mayor said would otherwise have paved about 1.2 miles of streets that residents had chosen.

What the vendors received is set out in the plan. The cooked-food and meat vendors were housed inside the renovated slaughterhouse, with running water and electricity paid for by the town council. The fish, fruit and vegetable vendors got temporary stalls beside the slaughterhouse, with some protection from the weather but responsibility for the security of their own goods overnight. Those who had traded between the market and the Cubanos area went to a temporary site pending a permanent one under a second phase. The council agreed to cover 14,990.68 Belize dollars of utilities and 24,530.00 in stall-fee arrears for all the temporarily relocated vendors for July 2012 to September 2014. At its August 2014 meeting the project steering committee approved reimbursements of stall fees to four of the relocated vendors, 6,955.00 Belize dollars in all, for July 2012 to April 2014.

The parking lot, where a large number of vendors had put up make-shift stalls, was to be taken back and the vendors moved into a new extension holding at most 22 stalls, one per family. The plan says five families are affected by that policy and names them: Zepeda, Carillo, Segura, Arzu and Sho. In the same paragraph it says temporary stalls will be erected beside the Cubanos area for those parking-lot vendors "who will be compensated with one or more stalls lost as a result of the Town Council’s one stall per family policy", and its table values the loss of the four parking-lot stall owners it names at one stall each and the loss of the other sixteen in the parking lot at none. A census of all the stall owners found that 56 per cent were women, that 70 per cent were of Mestizo ancestry in a town about 75 per cent of whose people are Garifuna, that 70 per cent paid between 15 and 22 Belize dollars a week for their stalls, and that weekly earnings ranged from 300 to 1,000 dollars in the parking lot to 900 to 3,000 dollars under the awnings. Fourteen sets of consultations were held with the vendors between April 2011 and July 2014.
cases.displaced_label: 20 market stall owners temporarily relocated, for 26 months, per the project's abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 40 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The plan's own figure is 20 vendors temporarily relocated, falling to 12 by July 2014 as most of those moved on to other parts of the town. The relocation was temporary and within Dangriga: nobody is recorded as having lost a home. The plan's table gives the length of the relocation as 26 months and lists the 20 by name across three groups: six under the awnings, four between the market and the Cubanos area and ten inside the market.
cases.outcome: The renovated market opened on 23 October 2014, Channel 5 Belize reported, after works that began in June 2012, with 44 stalls. The report gives the cost as 1,843,419.67 Belize dollars, above budget, with the first contractor paid about 800,000 before work stopped and the second contract costing roughly a million more. It quotes Mayor Swaso saying the building still lacked modern amenities and that some defects would be rectified, and says a government minister apologised to Dangriga residents for the delays. The project itself closed on 30 November 2016. The World Bank's completion report of 5 June 2017 says "All vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations, or compensated", and rates compliance with the social safeguard policies Satisfactory; neither it nor the evaluation review mentions the 25 per cent income loss the project's own action plan records.

cases.confidence_note: The 25 per cent income loss appears in two places eight months apart, but both trace to the same side. The project's own abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 reports it from an evaluation carried out jointly by the project implementation unit and the Dangriga Town Council. Channel 5 Belize reported it on 30 January 2014, while the works were still stopped, in the words of Mayor Gilbert Swaso: "The vendors continue to lose twenty-five percent of their income." Swaso heads the town council, which put up three per cent of the sub-project cost, paid the relocated vendors' utilities and was a party to the evaluation, so the press report is an independent publication of a figure the council itself produced rather than an independent measurement of it. What the Belizean press does corroborate independently is the harm around the figure: the works stopping in September 2013, the market staying shut, the change of contractor, the cost overrun and a government minister apologising to Dangriga residents for the delays. The plan itself names the twenty vendors, gives the length of their relocation as 26 months and marks each of their losses moderate. Two limits should be read with it. The relocation was temporary and within the town, and the first of the two evaluations, reported in April 2011, had concluded that most of those to be moved would not suffer a major loss of income or livelihood. The corruption and extortion allegations around the first contractor and the Social Investment Fund are allegations as the press reported them, not findings, and the employees concerned denied them. The two press reports differ on the first contractor: Amandala names him as Kenard Smart of K & G Construction and Channel 5 Belize as Kenard Smart of Corozal, and the plan names only "Mr. Smart". Amandala gives the second contract as 1,228,310.95 Belize dollars signed on 24 March 2014 while the plan gives the whole sub-project as 1,519,364.33 and Channel 5 Belize gives the final cost as about 1.84 million; the documents do not reconcile these.

cases.title: Land taken from 38 people for four West Bank power substations, with compensation unfinished when the works began
cases.place: Sarra village, Nablus Governorate, with almqeblih near Jenin, Beit Oula near Hebron and Qalandia near Ramallah, West Bank, Palestine
cases.point: Sarra village in Nablus Governorate, the site of one of the four substations. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Sarra. The land was taken at four separate sites, so this point stands for one of them.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank
lenders.role: Financed the four 161/33/22 kV substations, which were Component 1 of the project the World Bank appraised and the component the land was taken for. The completion report lists Component 1 as "financed by EIB" and records an original EIB loan of EUR 45 million effective in 2005 that was originally to finance two of the four substations, EUR 10 million of meters and part of the new distribution system, and that EIB restructured during implementation; EIB then had to secure internal approval of a EUR 44.5 million single-source contract for the construction of the four substations by the Israel Electric Corporation, signed in February 2012. The component's actual cost is given as US$56.5 million, mostly EIB with Norwegian funding for some auxiliary equipment (completion report, paragraphs 13, 25 and 26, and the donor contributions table). The World Bank's own grants paid for other components: the central distribution system, distribution rehabilitation, capacity building, consultancies and the start-up costs of the new transmission company and regulator.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Electric Utility Management Project, project number P084461, financed by two trust fund grants, TF-92336 and TF-94587. The original commitment was US$12.0 million and US$14.5 million was disbursed; the grant agreement for TF092336 is dated 30 June 2008 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, ICR00002455, 24 March 2017, data sheet and Annex 10). The Bank approved the project on 15 May 2008 and it closed on 30 September 2016, three years after the original closing date of 30 September 2013. The project was environmental Category B. The appraisal document's safeguard table marks two policies and only two: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), with Natural Habitats, Pest Management, Physical Cultural Resources, Indigenous Peoples, Forests, Safety of Dams, Projects in Disputed Areas and Projects on International Waterways all marked no (Project Appraisal Document, report no. 43298-62, 22 April 2008, section III.F). The Bank appraised the four substations as Component 1 of the project, and the abbreviated resettlement action plans for each substation were prepared under the Resettlement Policy Framework that the Palestinian Energy Authority wrote in 2008 and under World Bank guidelines (completion report, paragraph 30). In September 2013 a Bank supervision mission found the Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority non-compliant with Bank safeguard policies at three of the four substations, Jenin, Nablus and Hebron, because civil works had started before the Bank cleared and disclosed the environmental and resettlement instruments; the safeguards rating was upgraded to Moderately Satisfactory from Unsatisfactory in May 2014 and kept until closing (completion report, paragraph 30). In the same month a level-one restructuring adjusted the components, the objective and the indicators to the Bank-financed activities only. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group records that the Bank "continued to monitor safeguard compliance related to the high-voltage substations even after restructuring when these activities no longer formed part of the project", and that Bank-managed financing accounted for less than 10 per cent of the cost of the original project (ICR Review, section 8b). The completion report rates the project's overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory. The Bank's Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, on a split rating weighted by the 81 per cent of trust fund financing disbursed at restructuring, and rates risk to development outcome High (ICR Review, ICRR0020707, 2017, sections 6, 7 and 11a).

companies.name: Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority
companies.role: Implementing agency, the Palestinian Authority body responsible for the energy sector; its Project Management Unit ran the project. Its Land Acquisition Committee assessed the price of each parcel and a Land Evaluation Committee valued the land against neighbouring parcel prices; the expropriation decrees required cabinet approval and confirmation by the office of the president. This is the body the Bank's September 2013 mission found non-compliant with its safeguard policies at three of the four substations (completion report, paragraph 30; Resettlement Action Plan, March 2011, sections 2.2 and 2.3).

companies.name: Israel Electric Corporation
companies.role: Built the four substations under a single-source contract approved by the European Investment Bank. The completion report says the Palestinian Authority and EIB concluded that only this company could effectively build the substations in the West Bank, because of the complexity of the approval processes from the Israeli authorities and the need to deal with them, and that it took from May 2008 to October 2010 to agree contract terms, partly because the company had no obvious interest in speeding up construction, which would cut its short-term electricity sales to the West Bank (completion report, paragraph 25).

cases.community: Four high-voltage substations needed land at four sites. The project's Resettlement Action Plan of March 2011 names them and counts the people whose land was taken. At Jenin, 15,028 square metres were taken from 23 owners, including, in the plan's spelling, owners of almqeblih village; the plan says that process 'has already been conducted by Palestinian industrial Zone', that the ownership of the 15,028 square metres 'is transferred to PEA', and that JD 66,315.20, assessed at JD 4.41 per square metre, 'has to be paid for the 23 owner'. So the Jenin land was taken through the industrial zone and transferred on, not acquired by the energy authority itself. At Sarra village in Nablus Governorate, 15,174 square metres belonging to 10 owners, with JD 349,000 assessed at JD 23 per square metre to be paid. At Beit Oula village near Hebron, about 17,524 square metres from 4 owners, with JD 89,898 assessed at JD 5.13 per square metre to be paid. At Qalandia, 11,000 square metres bought directly, with one person listed as affected and no price yet set. The plan's summary table lists the four sites with 23, 10, 4 and 1 persons affected. It records the status of each: the Jenin process 'finish', Sarra and Beit Oula awaiting cabinet approval, Qalandia still at the estimation stage. The plan's two accounts of the Jenin site do not agree. Its summary table marks the Jenin status 'Resettlement process finish', while its annexed compensation table for the same three parcels enters 23 owners and JD 66,315.2 in the column for the amount awarded to owners, leaves the expropriation decree number and the expropriation date blank, and reads in the comments column: 'Assessed amount not yet awarded'. That annex also names each owner, with the parcel, the land title number, the area in dunams and a column for the owner's national identity card number: 23 people at Jenin across parcels 8/1, 10/1 and 11/1, in Almqebleh title 20010 and Berqin title 2, plus a 0.468-dunam road strip. The plan also lists tentative dates for Citizen Consultancy Meetings, Qalandia in September 2011 and Jenin, Nablus and Hebron in June 2012, after the assessments had been made; it describes those meetings as gathering community feedback on the configuration of the distribution system rather than on the land acquisition. For Sarra and Beit Oula the plan says notices with the owners' names and land titles were published twice in local newspapers and that no owner objected. The plan says the land was taken by expropriation under the 1953 Land Acquisition Law, applied in the West Bank from Jordanian legislation, and that it remains hard to seek remedies in the Palestinian court system because of uncertainty over enforcement and the limits of a court system operating under occupation. The project's completion report of 24 March 2017 records what happened next: at Jenin, Nablus and Hebron, civil works began before the Bank had cleared and disclosed the resettlement and environmental instruments, and 'project affected people were identified prior to construction and the compensation process had started but it had not yet been completed'. The same paragraph says the issue was solved thanks to the proactivity of the Bank team and for the benefit of EIB, and that the safeguards rating was upgraded in May 2014. A footnote to that paragraph records that the Bank's Jerusalem office received a complaint by email from the closest neighbour to the Nablus substation; the task team met the complainant, four other neighbours and the mayor, raised their concerns with the Palestinian authority and EIB, and sent the complainant a written response. The footnote does not say what the complaint was about. The areas, the owner counts and the assessed sums appear in that plan and in no outcome document. No document found counts anyone moved out of a home.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 38 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Resettlement Action Plan of March 2011 lists 38 persons affected across the four substation sites, in a table whose column is headed 'Number of person affected': 23 at Jenin, 10 at Sarra, 4 at Beit Oula and 1 at Qalandia. No document found counts anyone relocated, and the plan describes the parcels as land rather than housing.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2016. Three of the four substations were complete at closing; the fourth, at Ramallah, was 15 per cent complete, held up by permits from the Israeli authorities for works in Area C, and was planned for commissioning in July 2018. The two reports do not agree on where the compensation ended up. The completion report says the compensation process had started but had not yet been completed when the works began, and that the issue was solved. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the completion report reports that the non-compliance issues "had been rectified by closure", while adding that it does not state whether there was compliance with OP 4.01, and reads the same page as meaning that 'although project affected people were identified prior to the commencement of construction activities, the compensation process had not been completed by project closure', adds that the task team leader subsequently informed the Group that the process was later completed, and says the completion report does not state whether the compensation and resettlement processes conformed to the requirements of OP 4.12. The statement that the process was completed is attributed to Bank staff, not to any document.

cases.community: The project built water and sewerage networks, treatment plants and pumping stations in Ahwaz and Shiraz. The completion report of 31 March 2010 gives one site where land was taken from people. For pumping station AS23-1 on Jomhori Boulevard in Ahwaz, a plot of 800 square metres, the land 'was a residential house that belonged to two individual owners and agreement with them was reached, a down payment was paid, and the property was expropriated'. The report then says: 'Since the deal involved resettlement of at least eight individuals, an abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) was prepared.' The report does not say whether the balance of the price was paid, where the eight went, or what they received beyond the price of the house. It says Land Acquisition Plans were prepared wherever land was expropriated and Resettlement Action Plans wherever resettlement of people or displacement of livelihoods was involved, and that several resettlement and land acquisition reviews were carried out during implementation. The same paragraph of the completion report says the environmental impact of the investments was generally positive and that there were no compliance issues in either Ahwaz or Shiraz. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 September 2010 says that, according to the completion report, there was adequate compliance with social safeguards policies and procedures in both cities. The appraisal document of 29 April 2004 had said of the expropriations it listed: 'In no case are residences or current economic activities or livelihoods affected.' What it listed for Ahwaz was an unused agricultural plot of 67 hectares from 13 local farmers, with compensation then being negotiated, and eight pumping-station plots of which two were privately owned, all of it described as undeveloped urban land; its Ahwaz annex adds 'There are no holders of other rights, no relocation or loss of shelter, income, or livelihoods.' The appraisal figure is 67 hectares in the document's text and 67.5 hectares in its own expropriation table. No outcome document found says what happened to those 13 owners. cases.displaced_note: No count of people relocated is entered for this case. ICIJ gives 8 for the project, which is its count of project-affected people. The completion report's own figure, in its safeguards section, is that the expropriation of the house for pumping station AS23-1 'involved resettlement of at least eight individuals'. 'At least eight' is a floor rather than a count, and the sentence records that an abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan was prepared because the deal involved their resettlement rather than that eight people were moved, so the figure stays uncounted. No other count of people moved appears anywhere in the project's documents.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2009 with the project unfinished. The completion report says critical components, including treatment plants, pumping stations and pipes, were incomplete or under construction and not fully operational, that unaccounted-for water deteriorated in Ahwaz, and that the financial position of both water companies worsened. It says lack of completion 'will disproportionately affect the poorer segments of the society' because most of the remaining components sit in poor neighbourhoods. Where it makes the same point in the present tense, in the list of risks, it adds in the next sentence that the proportion of completed works is also higher in poorer neighbourhoods, given the project's focus on the poor. The Independent Evaluation Group's review puts it as lack of completion having 'disproportionately affected the poorer segments of society'. No later document was found on the house at Jomhori Boulevard or on the eight people.

The six is the resettlement plan's own count. The resettlement plan of May 2011 listed 27 structures or plots and said 27 people would be affected, with no permanent or temporary structure lost and no land acquisition needed; it described the effects as temporary inconvenience. The completion report says that in June 2013, two years after the plan was written, implementation had not started, and that the number of people affected was then listed as 15, entitled to about US$1,500 in all. That 15 is also the plan's figure, and in the plan it is not a count of people: the plan says it "covered 15 shops and 4 residential houses which will be impacted by the project", and its Annex 1 lists 15 entitlement entries by initials or trading name — among them a petrol station, an inn, a lumber shop, a charcoal and firewood seller and two concrete-products sites — with a disturbance allowance and assistance for each and a total of 37,923.49 dalasi. Radio announcements in local languages and repeated visits followed, and "Compensation was provided to the six people who were located." A footnote cites a monitoring report of 7 October 2014 from the ministry and a supervision mission report of January 2015 acknowledging payment to just six of the 15. The report says many of the others had moved away and that different businesses were on the sites. cases.community: The loans paid for fibre optic links including Booué to Koumameyong, Lalara, Mitzic, Oyem, Bitam and the Cameroon border. The completion report says the project's overall safeguards rating was lowered to Moderately Satisfactory in the final status report for three reasons: delays in the safeguards audit; "social risks associated with non-compensation for the accidental destruction of assets during fieldwork in Lalara"; and incomplete implementation of the Indigenous Peoples Plan in the field. A footnote adds that the construction operators were asked to compensate those destructions but had not done so by the closing date, "raising the prospects of complaints from people whose assets were destroyed". A second footnote says some indigenous peoples activities were still not carried out. The grievance mechanism was working at the closing date and followed the two environmental and social management plans, but its last revision did not cover gender-based violence. 168 complaints were received, 41 per cent of them about loss of revenue and stalls, and 129 had been resolved by the date of a unit report of 11 March 2021. The government's own account, printed in the completion report, says counterpart funds of around FCFA 3 billion made it possible to compensate project-affected persons, repair non-conformities and finish the works, and that local communities helped resolve complaints during resettlement operations and provided land for the technical centres. No document counts the people whose assets were destroyed at Lalara.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 13 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document counts anyone relocated.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 October 2020 with the Lalara destructions uncompensated and the Indigenous Peoples Plan unfinished, and with 129 of the 168 complaints recorded as resolved in a project unit report of 11 March 2021 and the rest still being processed. The Evaluation Group's review says both the Lalara compensation and the indigenous peoples issue were still unresolved when it was written, attributing that to the project team rather than to a document.

lenders.name: World Bank (International Development Association)
lenders.role: Project P079749, West Africa Regional Transport and Transit Facilitation Project. IDA Credits 44350 (Mali), 44380 (Burkina Faso) and 44390 (Ghana), original commitment SDR 116.70 million, revised SDR 116.00 million, of which SDR 115.43 million was disbursed. Approved 19 June 2008, closing date 30 June 2015 (completion report ICR00003592, 31 December 2015; Financing Agreements for Credit 4438-BF conformed 8 July 2008, Credit 4439-GH conformed 11 July 2008 and Credit 4435-ML conformed 17 July 2008). Environmental category B. Two safeguard policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP/GP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12); the Evaluation Group's assessment report says the second was triggered only for minor land acquisition or loss of income from the road rehabilitation or the construction of the rest stops. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's field-based assessment report of 19 April 2018 rates borrower performance moderately satisfactory and says the supervision of safeguards was satisfactory. Parallel financing came from the African Development Bank, the European Union and the West African Development Bank.

companies.role: The ministry that published the compensation and resettlement framework for the Malian sections of the corridor and held the Bamako to Bougouni and Sikasso to Hérémakono works.

companies.role: The roads agency, under Ghana's transport ministry, responsible for the Ghanaian corridor works and the land acquisition for the rest stops.

cases.community: The credits rehabilitated road sections on the corridor from the port of Tema in Ghana through Ouagadougou to Bamako, and were to build rest stops. The completion report says that "the compensations were fully carried out, albeit with delays. Particularly in Burkina Faso, the works contract was signed while the compensations were still ongoing." In Ghana an increase in the financing let the resettlement and compensation, first budgeted from government funds, be paid faster. "In the case of Mali, involuntary resettlements were made for seven households. The compensations were fully financed from the counterpart funding resources." The Evaluation Group's field-based assessment report says all compensation payments were made, with delays in Burkina Faso and Ghana caused by government budget limits, that in Mali seven households were resettled and compensation was timely, and that "no information was obtained on how many people were compensated in Burkina Faso and Ghana". It names slow land acquisition in Ghana for the rest stops as the only shortcoming of the safeguards work. The abbreviated compensation plan for the Ouagadougou to Sakoinsé section, written in October 2007, names four people losing a hectare of land each and 800 kilogrammes of harvest a year at borrow pit 4 and at Douré and Sakoinsé, and lists trees lost at two other borrow pits. The borrower's own report, printed as an annex to the completion report, lists delays in payment of compensation and counterpart funds, and land acquisition, among the project's challenges.
cases.killed_note: The completion report says the road safety measures considerably reduced the number of accidents along the corridor without reaching the targets, and the borrower's annex says the speed humps built on the Ouagadougou to Sakoinsé section reduced deaths on that stretch. Neither document records a death caused by the works.
cases.displaced_label: 7 households resettled in Mali, from the completion report (paragraph 67, 31 December 2015) and the Evaluation Group's assessment report (paragraph 4.6, 19 April 2018)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 9 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The seven households are the only count of people resettled in any document; the assessment report says no information was obtained on how many people were compensated in Burkina Faso or Ghana.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2015. Both the completion report and the assessment report record all the compensation as eventually paid. The transit facilitation part of the project failed: the three countries never agreed on the customs arrangements.

Approved 26 May 2005, original closing 30 September 2010, actual closing 30 June 2012 after three restructurings, the last on 22 February 2012 (completion report ICR2521, 21 December 2012). Environmental category B. Five safeguard policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP 4.04), Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11), Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome High, and Bank and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. companies.name: Unité de Coordination de Projets (UCoP), Democratic Republic of the Congo
companies.role: The government project coordination unit that implemented the project. The completion report says a lack of oversight by it led to the corruption case the Bank's integrity unit investigated, and the borrower's own report names inadequate monitoring of environmental and social aspects during construction among the weaknesses a technical audit found.

companies.name: Bureau Central de Coordination (BCECO), Democratic Republic of the Congo
companies.role: One of the delegated contract managers for the works; it was trained by an international environmental and social consulting firm hired after the mid-term review.

cases.community: The grant rehabilitated National Road 6 from Akula through Gemena and Mbari to Libenge and Zongo in Équateur and National Road 5 from Lubumbashi through Kasomeno to Kasenga in Katanga, and funded urban works in several towns. The completion report says the mid-term review "revealed that project affected persons resettled due to the road construction were not adequately compensated, that the works contracts did not, as foreseen, include funding to mitigate environmental aspects, and that the problem of medical wastes from health facilities funded by the project was not fully taken into account". An international environmental and social consulting firm was then hired to train the project unit, the contractors and the delegated contract manager, and management plans were drawn up for each 30-kilometre road segment. A total of 627 project-affected persons were compensated. At project closing the beneficiary satisfaction survey found no adequate solution to the medical waste. The report also covers National Road 2, rehabilitated under an earlier Bank-financed project: no displacement or asset losses occurred there, but the road shoulders were cut back, leaving almost no space between the road and neighbouring buildings and raising the risk of traffic accidents. An after-the-fact resettlement plan was prepared for that road and was to be paid for by this project, but a change in the lender's rules stopped cash compensation being paid from its funds. The government has implemented the plan as money became available and had paid 61 per cent of the amount due to 35 project-affected persons. The amount is given as US$262,090 in the completion report and as US$202,090 in the Evaluation Group's review. The Group's review adds that an indigenous peoples plan was prepared and circulated to non-governmental organisations, academics, Pygmy associations and news agencies, and that no information is given on whether it was carried out.
cases.killed_note: No document records a death caused by the works. The completion report says the reduced shoulders on National Road 2 increase the risk of traffic accidents.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives no displacement estimate for this project. No document counts people relocated. The 627 is a count of project-affected persons compensated, and the 35 a count of people owed money for the earlier National Road 2 works.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2012. At that point 61 per cent of the National Road 2 compensation had been paid to 35 people and the rest was being paid by the government as funds allowed; the medical waste problem was unsolved. The completion report also records a corruption case investigated by the lender's integrity unit, and an advance of US$1.4 million on a road contract cancelled in 2010 for non-performance that had still not been repaid when the report was written.

fields_add.community: The Bank's own completion report, dated 27 April 2016, sets out the case under project number P086807, credit agreement C4083-AL. It says the Executive Directors authorised the Panel investigation on 1 November 2007 and that the residents of Jale filed several complaints. The requesters said the Construction Police of the Municipality of Vlora had demolished their permanent residences in whole or in part, that the police singled out Jale while sparing other similar buildings along the coast because public officials wanted to clear space for a resort at and around the site, and that the Bank had failed to supervise the work it was financing.
fields_add.outcome: Bank management told the Board there was no direct or indirect link between the project and the demolitions, and said they were part of a government programme that had started in 2001. The Panel concluded that the decision not to apply the resettlement policy at appraisal and during implementation was a root cause in the mishandling of the demolitions. Management then acknowledged "serious errors in project preparation and supervision, along with errors in communication with the Board of the World Bank". It agreed to pay the requesters' legal costs for a case-by-case legal review of the April 2007 demolitions, to appoint an independent observer to monitor that review, and to apply assistance packages retroactively to poor and vulnerable people affected by the demolitions. A footnote was added to the Bank's resettlement policy stating that the policy does not apply to land use planning activities unless they involve Bank-assisted investments that require the taking of land. The completion report of April 2016 says the project had disbursed only about 25 per cent before the investigation, that the suspension of disbursements lasted 17 months and was lifted in June 2010, and that the project closed on 31 March 2015.

sources_add.title: Sri Lanka - Metro Colombo Urban Development Project (P122735): Implementation Completion and Results Report
Rehabilitation of St. Sebastian South Canal: Resettlement Action Plan, Project Management Unit, Metro Colombo Urban Development Project (SFG1314)
NHSL flooding: Officials blame 8 houses blocking new drain (The Morning, Methmalie Dissanayake)

fields_add.community: The Bank's completion report for the project (P122735), published on 14 December 2022, puts the total at 652 households affected by the project, through acquisition of private land, recovery of state land occupied by squatter households and the relocation of project-affected households, 'largely the non-titleholder squatter families living along canal banks'. It gives no count of households actually relocated. The same figure of 91 appears as a target in the project's own Resettlement Action Plan for St. Sebastian South Canal, dated 8 August 2013 and updated August 2014, which counts 91 squatter households and says it 'is a regulatory requirement that these 91 households are relocated'; it sets a target of resettling them by September 2014 in individual flats in the condominium at 66 Watte, each flat of 400 square feet and valued in the plan at LKR 7 million, with a transport allowance of LKR 5,000 each. The plan says the 91 households had expressed willingness to relocate and that about eighty of the 91 would see no adverse impact on their livelihood activities. That is a plan and not an outcome, and no Bank document found counts how many actually moved. The completion report names two resettlement sites in use, Methsanda Sevana and Siyasetha Sevana, where women hold four of five and four of six of the building management positions, and records vulnerability allowances of LKR 12.3 million paid to 56 female-headed households living around the drainage works. It also records a second site where people were required to leave their homes. At Norris Canal, completing the works required the relocation of 24 households in a building belonging to the Colombo Municipal Council, which was 'structurally too weak to withstand the deep excavation works, and thus complete demolition was required'. The report describes those 24 as 16 tenants and 8 legal owners holding freehold title under a council deed, then says eight tenants were in the process of relocating because the Supreme Court had decided they should vacate the building, and that the council's acquisition of the properties of 'the four legal owners' under the Land Acquisition Act was in its early stages. The report does not explain the gap between the eight legal owners and the four. At project closure this sub-project was unfinished, with 126 metres of the 675-metre Norris Canal diversion not built, and the government agreed to finance the completion of that balance; the report says the project had followed the resettlement process in the plan, that there was no safeguards non-compliance, and that the Bank would continue to monitor the progress of the remaining resettlement. The project's grievance mechanism recorded 407 grievances in the Bank's text and 423 in the borrower's own section of the same report; 377 were resolved, and the report says the rest were largely about compensation for construction-related damage and would be settled by the contractors through their insurers.
fields_add.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2021 and the Bank's completion report, dated 14 December 2022, rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest, on a loan of which US$199.06 million of the original US$213 million was disbursed. The Norris Canal resettlement was still unsettled five years after closure, on works the government had agreed to finance. On 10 November 2026 officials told the Colombo District Coordination Committee that a new drainage route built along Arnold Ratnayake Mawatha towards Beira Lake, to relieve the Norris Canal's insufficient discharge capacity, had 'stalled 100 to 150 metres short of completion because eight structures occupied the stretch', after flash floods on 6 November flooded the ground floors of the National Hospital of Sri Lanka. The residents had been offered alternative housing valued at Rs 5 million and then at about Rs 11 million, and refused both. An official said: 'Since these residents refuse to vacate even after being allocated housing options, we will proceed under the said Act,' meaning the Land Acquisition Act, and Prime Minister Harini Amarasuriya replied: 'Let us proceed accordingly under the Act.' She called for a task force of the Colombo Municipal Council, the District Secretariat, the Urban Development Authority, the police and the armed forces, and a joint meeting on 13 November to make binding decisions on removing unauthorised construction blocking drains.
fields_add.confidence_note: Added in round 32: the Bank's completion report of 14 December 2022 is now the source for the project-wide total of 652 affected households and for the 24 households at Norris Canal. The Morning's report of 11 November 2026 names the same canal, calling it an unfinished drainage project on the Norris Canal blocked by eight houses, and independently records the housing offers those occupants refused and the government's decision to use the Land Acquisition Act; it does not mention the World Bank, and the tie between the works and the loan is that the completion report names the same canal and the same unfinished stretch. Whether the newspaper's eight structures are the completion report's eight legal owners, or its eight relocating tenants, is not stated in either source. The works left to finish were ones the government agreed at closure to pay for, after the loan had closed. The two accounts of the unfinished length differ and are left as each gives them: 126 metres of 675 in the completion report, 100 to 150 metres in the newspaper. No count of households actually relocated appears in any Bank document for this project.
